en: Preface to the Collected Commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*:
In the eighth month of the year Wuli (1605), I was with Dong Xuanzai attending upon the Great Master Zibo at Mount She in Jinling.
Daily we engaged in long discussions on the unborn (*anutpāda*), and I remarked that "sitting rigidly in silent illumination" constitutes heterodox Chan. It is not...
"It is impossible for us two to deeply navigate the ocean of the teachings. One day, atop the pavilion of Dharma Master Suanan, he obtained a small Sanskrit manuscript and showed a look of joy.
He handed it to the two of us with his own hands, saying, "If you wish to deeply navigate the ocean of the teachings, then this is the vessel, the rudder, and the oars.
Upon examining it, we found it to be the *Nyāyapraveśa* (Treatise on Entering Correct Reasoning). We two were at a loss, not knowing what to do.
That is to say: Huanzhai, the successor of Suan’an, once spoke on this himself. The Master ordered him to explain it for the two of us, yet he was ultimately unable to clarify it;
Xuanzai knit his brows in distress and departed. I personally recorded one sheet of notes and briefly organized them into topical divisions.
I tucked it away in my satchel. At the end of the year, while traveling to the capital for the imperial examination, I visited Master Mìzàng at his monastic quarters together with Yú Zhōngfǔ.
Upon seeing a book on a table, I casually opened it to look; it was a commentary on this treatise. When I inquired about it, I learned it was the pen of Dharma Master Huànjū.
Consequently, I entrusted Zhōngfǔ to transcribe a copy so that I might read it during my leisure time, even though it was already clear [to me].
Huanzhai remarked, "It remains obscure as before. Thereafter, whenever he encountered a lecture hall, he invariably inquired first about this treatise.

Everyone said, "Since the time of Master Xuanzang, this treatise has been renowned as the most profound and difficult to comprehend; moreover, the ancient commentaries have been lost, and there is no longer a lineage of transmission for its exposition.
It is truly difficult to reach a definitive judgment through mere conjecture. Consequently, I ceased to apply my mind to it for a long time. Thus it was.
In the summer of the You year, while I was in the Southern Office, I encountered the commentary by Master Cheng of Shiziwo in the study of my fellow official He Ju.
Although it appeared to clarify matters further than [the work of] Huanju, its meaning was rather shallow and narrow; thus, I held it in low regard. In the summer of the Renzi year...
The Dharma Master Yunpu held the retreat within my Zhuyin Garden and presented me with his commentary on this treatise.
While I lay prostrate in bed with no mind for activity, I was able to read it at leisure. Upon opening the volume, it was clear to me;

it possesses a definitive perspective that is not comparable to the mere conjectures or derivative interpretations of others. It even takes the arguments of Nāgārjuna and compares them with the citations from Qingliang and Yongming.
I examined the words of the commentaries and sub-commentaries, cross-referencing and verifying them against one another; thus, there were also points of contradiction.

Thereupon, I investigated by day and contemplated by night, studying without ceasing until I forgot both sleep and food. It was as if sitting in a dark room that gradually brightens after a long time.
Now, I see all the objects within the room with perfect clarity; even a needle or a thread no longer causes me any confusion.
Therefore, having collected various treatises relevant to this subject and harmonizing them with the commentaries of the three masters, I have once again provided a detailed explanation.
It began on the eleventh day of the fifth month and was completed on the twentieth day of that same month. Alas! This treatise...
This is merely a matter of establishing and refuting according to the established rules; it contains no subtle words or profound meanings that require awakening to become clear.

Furthermore, although the ancient commentaries and sub-commentaries cannot be fully verified, they are scattered here and there in various places. Even by collecting these remaining fragments, one is still sufficient to illuminate the meaning.
Moreover, every single character and phrase therein has its own provenance, as they too are scattered throughout various treatises.

How could one possibly resort to such arbitrary judgment? For those who study this treatise, the danger does not lie in the loss of the transmission; rather, the danger lies in a lack of profound reflection and extensive investigation.
I am but a common scholar (*cuodà*) who has reached white hair while fleeing into the Chan school; moreover, I have long been afflicted by illness.

Regarding this treatise, I am like one peering at the heavens through a tube or fathoming the ocean with a shell—how could I dare claim to have achieved profound reflection and extensive investigation? As for my persistent and earnest [explanations], they are as follows:
This work is undertaken because I myself am fully aware of my own incapacity, yet I have placed great hope in the various masters;

rather than resting content with what has already been attained, I have striven further toward that which remains unattained. The majority of the established doctrines cited herein are drawn from the works of others, and thus it is titled *Jishie* (Collected Explanations) to indicate that these are not my own views.
Occasionally, there are instances where I point out the errors of others to clarify my own correctness, but this was truly out of necessity.

Thus, the various doctrines became confused, leaving scholars wandering aimlessly and bewildered as to which path to follow, like those lost on a journey who have just begun to ask others for directions when their first informant fails to speak clearly.
Is this not failing to guide them onto the correct path, but instead sitting idly by while they remain lost?
Long ago, before Master Xuanzang had yet reached India, Mañjuśrī warned him: [text continues]
He stopped Śīlabhadra from taking his own life and waited for him to arrive. When he had not yet returned, he again alerted him to hasten back.
It is evident that this region and this school share a profound karmic affinity; what was obscured has been made manifest once more, and what was severed has been restored.
It is precisely at this moment that we must exert our own strength.

All who participate in this school shall one day be among those gathered for the single assembly of the Dragon Flower; if they are not, let us together cast them out, and if they are, let us together follow them.

There is no distinction between "self" and "other," nor any comparison of long and short. Furthermore, one must not engage in idle chatter for the sake of protecting one's own feelings of pain and grief;
since there is neither self nor other, nor long nor short, to do otherwise would entail the fault of both deluding oneself and others.

One cannot even escape the retribution of the three miserable realms, let alone hope to become a lamb or a pheasant in the presence of Maitreya. If these words are not true, then this [practice] is not true.
The tongue shall be extracted.
Written with great effort despite illness by the lay practitioner Wang Kengtang on the day before the summer solstice in the year Renzi,
the fortieth year of the Wanli era.
*The Commentary on the Entrance into Logic for Entering into Correct Theory*, compiled by Wang Kengtang of Jintan.
△ The structural outline is divided into four parts. First, the explanation of the title. Regarding "Logic" (*hetuvidyā*): the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states that a bodhisattva seeks...
"Dharma. Where should it be sought? It should be sought within all five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*). What are the five fields of knowledge? They are:

the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*), the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), and the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*).
These are detailed in the *Śrutamayī-bhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Regarding the explanation of the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*):"
That is to say, among all things and established phenomena within the investigation of meaning, these are called "the objects of investigation.
The phenomena that accord with them are called "all things. All things are precisely *hetuvidyā* (logic), because they serve as the cause for illuminating the investigation of meaning.
Furthermore, it is said that herein there are briefly seven types: first, the essence of debate; second, debate... [and so forth].
The locus; the basis for the three treatises; the adornment of the four treatises; the grounds for defeat in debate; the transcendence through debate;

and the many functions of debate. Within this present treatise, there are eight gates and two benefits, which correspond to one of the seven types—the "basis for the treatises"—while the other six types, such as "essential nature," are already contained therein.
Through the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), one is able to enter [the truth].
"Entering into the correct principle. "Entering" refers to the harmonious correspondence of understanding and realization, wherein the subject and object are in perfect accord.

There are two kinds of causes: the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) and the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*). The productive cause is like a seed producing a sprout; the revealing cause is like a lamp illuminating an object.

However, these two types of causes each have three aspects. As for the three aspects of the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*): first, the verbal productive cause; second, the cognitive productive cause;

and third, the objective productive cause. As for the three aspects of the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*): first, the cognitive revealing cause; second, the verbal revealing cause; and third, the objective revealing cause.

When a cause possesses these three characteristics, it is called the "correct cause" (*samyag-hetu*). "Illumination" (*vidyā*) refers to correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), which pervades both cause and effect. Regarding the cause:
"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to that which initially measures; "resultant knowledge" (*phala-jñāna*) refers to that which ultimately and definitively realizes.

"Correct principle" (*nyāya*) means that within both mundane and supramundane phenomena, the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—each possess their own natural and inherent logic. Because it is free from all error and inversion, it is called "correct.
For example, taking the first three [elements] as the cause for establishing that form (*rūpa*) is certainly not subsumed by the eye-faculty.

When separated from visual consciousness, the three characteristics remain unimpaired; this then reveals the correct principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). [The formal inference is: "True and universally established form" is the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is certainly not separate from visual consciousness. The reason (*hetu*) is:

because it is admitted by oneself to be included within the first three [realms] and is not subsumed under the eye [organ]. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is like visual consciousness. An explanation of this will follow in a later passage.

By taking dependent origination as the reason, one establishes the thesis that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This then reveals the correct principle of the conditioned. [The formal inference is: "Conditioned phenomena" is the subject. The thesis is that they are certainly empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.

Thesis: [Unconditioned phenomena] are not substantially existent. Reason: Because they do not arise. Similar Example: Like a flower in the sky. [Just as] a flower in the sky does not arise and has no substantial reality, so too unconditioned phenomena do not arise and likewise have no substantial reality.
[This establishes the correct principle of the unconditioned. (The formal syllogism is: Unconditioned phenomena are the subject;

they definitely lack substantial reality is the property of the subject; the reason is "because they do not arise"; the similar example is "like a flower in the sky. A flower in the sky has no arising; a flower in the sky has no reality; unconditioned phenomena have no arising; unconditioned phenomena also have no reality. [End of excerpt]

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-tilaka-śāstra* (Treatise on the Jewel in the Hand of the Mahāyāna) explains that this treatise exclusively elucidates these two types of inference (*anumāna*). Since one enters into correct reasoning through the illumination provided by the reasons (*hetu*), it is called "Hetuvidyā" (Logic), which means "Entering Correct Reasoning by Means of Reasons.
Although there are three members of a syllogism (*trirūpa*), it is specifically termed "Hetuvidyā" because the reason possesses the power [to establish the conclusion].
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is not manifested without a reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not established without a reason;

therefore, the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) within the reason—namely, that it is entirely a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharmatva*), its necessary presence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and its total absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*)—encompass the thesis.

Furthermore, these three members, when viewed in relation to the resulting fruit of knowledge they produce, are collectively termed the "reason. Thus, the subsequent text states: "By virtue of that serving as the cause..."

Regarding the object of inference, correct knowledge arises; therefore, it is known that when the reason (*hetu*) is presented, the three members [of the syllogism] are complete. An ancient commentary asks:

"In establishing a formal argument (*vāda*), when the three members are fulfilled, the result (*phala*) is clearly understood without being explicitly stated; why then do you speak only of 'Reason-knowledge' (*Hetuvidyā*)? The answer provides two interpretations:
First, when presenting an argument against an opponent, the three members of the proof (*sādhana*) are fully present. It is through these that the opponent generates knowledge. [...]

Both are termed "cause" (*hetu*). That which is produced [by the cause] is called "knowledge" (*vidyā*). Because reason (*li*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) are mentioned together, it is called *hetuvidyā* (Logic).

Second, within the context of inference (*anumāna*), there is that which is accepted and that which is not yet accepted. To establish what is not yet accepted, there must necessarily be a means of establishment;
this means of establishment is the "cause," and that which is established is the "result. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is revealed by the cause, whereby its meaning becomes clear. This...

Thus, cause and effect are both clearly manifested, and there is no contradiction or obstruction in principle. The Great Master Ci'en said: "The *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* was originally taught solely by the Buddha;

its texts are extensive and its meanings are dispersed throughout the various sūtras. At the beginning of the kalpa, Akṣapāda first established the categories of the 'real' (*tattva*) and the 'semblance' (*pratibhāsa*)."
Thereupon Vasubandhu restated the rules and models; yet, although the governing framework was established, the subtle nuances remained undifferentiated.

Consequently, even as the proponent and opponent engaged in mutual exposition, there was still uncertainty regarding the principles of establishing and refuting arguments. Then there appeared the Bodhisattva Dignāga, one of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Concealing his traces among the mountain thickets and dwelling in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the peaks, he contemplated the benefits of composing this treatise.
[He] examined the profusion and concision of the text and its meaning. At that time, the mountain crags shook with a roar and the clouds and mists shifted their colors.
A mountain deity lifted the Bodhisattva’s feet several hundred feet into the air and proclaimed: "The Buddha taught the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), yet its profound mystery is difficult to fathom.
Since the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, its great significance has been lost and severed. Now, fortunately, [you] possess vast wisdom and have deeply penetrated the sacred intent of the *Hetuvidyā*."
They discussed the Path and requested that he propagate it once again. The Bodhisattva then emitted a divine light that illuminated those whose faculties were ready for conversion.

At that time, the King of Andhra in South India, seeing the emission of this light, suspected that [the Bodhisattva] had entered the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) and requested proof that he had attained the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

The Bodhisattva said: "I have entered meditative concentration to observe [reality], and I am about to explain profound sūtras; my heart aspires toward Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), not [to the fruit of Arhatship]."
“I wish for the fruit of the Lesser Vehicle. The King said, “The fruit of No-more-learning is that which all the noble ones revere; I pray that you, Venerable One, will quickly realize it.

The Bodhisattva patted him, wishing to fulfill the King’s request. Then, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī snapped his fingers to alert him, saying, “Why do you abandon the Great Mind and instead give rise to a lesser resolve?
To bring about vast benefit, you should turn the *Yogācāra* teachings spoken by Maitreya to rectify [the world].”

The collapsing moral order was rectified, and the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) was established to restore the standards of discipline. Dignāga respectfully received his instructions and followed them in practice;
thereupon, he applied himself with profound reflection and rigorous study, composing the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (The Gate of Right Reasoning). As for "Right Reasoning" (*nyāya*):
The meaning of the fundamental, true essence of all phenomena (*dharmas*). As for "gate" (*mukha*), it refers to the means by which one employs the scales of wisdom to illuminate and understand.
Based on this, it appears that this treatise is the "means of entry" (*praveśaka*), while Dignāga’s treatise is the "object of entry" (*praveśya*).

Within the Tripiṭaka, there are two translations of the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Gate of Right Reasoning); these were composed by the Bodhisattva Ārya Nāgārjuna, whereas Dignāga’s treatise is not [found therein].
This can be verified. △ Next, regarding the author:
composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin.
"Śaṅkarasvāmin" has not yet been seen translated [into Chinese]. The postscript states: "There was a Bodhisattva Devendra; he is now explained."
Consequently, Śaṅkara was taken as the term for "Heaven" (天). However, the Sanskrit word for heaven is *deva*;
perhaps all four characters [of the name] were originally Sanskrit. *Bodhisattva* is fully rendered as *bodhisattva*, which here means "Awakened Being" (覺有情).
It is a designation for one who unites compassion and wisdom to benefit both self and others. △ Third, the translators.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Emperor Gaozu of Tang, Li Yuan, served as the Regional Inspector (Liushiu) of Taiyuan and was subsequently enfeoffed as the Duke of Tang. Later, he obtained the empire, and thus "Tang" became the name of the state.
As for the "Tripitaka," it consists of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras. The life and deeds of the Dharma Master are fully recorded in the Cien [Monastery] records.
Commentary: Having obtained this treatise and the details regarding its translation, the subsequent preface is now complete. IV. The Main Text, in four parts:
1. The Verse:

The means of proof (*sādhana*) and the means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), As well as their fallacious counterparts (*tad-ābhāsa*), are solely for the purpose of awakening others; Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

Regarding this single verse, which begins with "And that which resembles [the true proof] is realized only by oneself," there are eight meanings in total. First, the "true *sādhana*" (this indicates the name; the following explains its meaning).

This refers to extending a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) against an opponent (this explains the two characters "true *sādhana*"). It consists of the three members being complete and lucid ("complete" means they are not deficient; "lucid" means they are not erroneous; this explains the character "true"). Because it brings about understanding in others.

(1) Because the thesis established is true, it can produce the fruit of knowledge in others (the opposite of this may be understood from below). (2) True refutation: this refers to the rejection of another's constituent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being incomplete or erroneous, thereby demonstrating and awakening the opponent.

(3) Fallacious establishment: this refers to presenting a means of valid cognition against an adversary while lacking one of the three members or containing errors, thus failing to inform the adversary.
(4) Fallacious refutation: this refers to falsely rejecting another's means of valid cognition as being incomplete or erroneous.
Because one does not awaken to the subject, there are five types of true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

These refer to the arising of correct cognition regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*), which operates within its own characteristics; this is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that attains the intrinsic nature of the object.

Sixth is true inference (*anumāna*), which refers to observing an object by means of various signs (such as knowing fire upon seeing smoke), because corresponding cognition arises. Seventh is pseudo-direct perception, which refers to conceptual cognition regarding...

The "transformation of meaning" (arthānyathātva) occurs because one perceives [an object] without it corresponding to its actual reality. This includes the cognition of jars, clothes, and so forth—since jars and clothes are merely conventional aggregations and are not objects of true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The eighth is "pseudo-inference" (*tarka-ābhāsa*), which refers to the arising of a contradictory understanding regarding the object to be inferred due to a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Regarding the two benefits—awakening others and awakening oneself: "awakening others" means that through the means of establishment (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), one is able to illuminate meanings not yet understood by others.

Therefore, regarding "self-awakening": because it can induce the two types of wisdom that differentiate between existence and non-existence through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), self-awakening and awakening others appear to follow this same principle.
Next, the commentary on the eight verses of the *kārikā* follows.
Thus, the essential meaning of all treatises is summarized in this single verse.
Although there are many treatises, their essential meanings do not transcend the rules for establishing and refuting based on the eight gates and two benefits.
Among these eight, the first is the gate of the true means of proof (*sādhana*). First—
This provides a general indication of the three members.

Herein, the multiple statements such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth are called the "proof" (*sādhana*). This is because the multiple statements consisting of the thesis, reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) reveal the meaning that has not yet been understood by those who raise questions.

The phrase "in this context" (*atra*) signifies the commencement of the treatise, or it carries the sense of selection and retention. It is called "in this context" because it occurs within the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth. "Selection" (*viveka*) means excluding others; "retention" (*dhāraṇa*) means maintaining one's own position.
This serves to distinguish [this work] from other treatises and to maintain what ought to be explained within this very treatise.

The first sentence cites the phenomenon (*dharma*) to indicate its name. Regarding "the thesis and so forth" (*pakṣādi*), the "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*). There are two types of proof (*sādhana*): first, [the thesis...].

The three members constitute the proof (*sādhana*). They receive the name "proof" in relation to the questioner; the two—reason (*hetu*) and example (*udāharaṇa*)—receive the name "proof" in relation to the thesis (*pakṣa*).
This refers to the meaning explained previously. Therefore, it concludes: "These three parts are called the proof.

From the phrase "by means of the thesis," etc., it is established that they are called "proof" because they are addressed to the questioner. By revealing what was not yet understood, one brings about the awakening of the other.
△ Fourth: A Separate Exposition of the Three Branches. Part One: The Thesis (*pakṣa*).

Herein, the thesis refers to a subject (*dharmin*) that is commonly recognized and a predicate (*viśeṣaṇa*) that is commonly recognized, which, by virtue of their distinct nature, are intended by oneself as the property to be proven (*sādhyatva*).
This is called the thesis. For example, "Sound is impermanent" is established as a thesis.

In this context, regarding the "true means of proof" (*sādhana*), the term *pakṣa* (thesis/position) has two meanings. That which is the object of adherence is called the *pakṣa*; it signifies the "master" (*prabhu*).

That which is capable of being adhered to is called the *pakṣa*; it signifies that which is "esteemed" (*pūjita*). Taking as its master the sense of what one personally cherishes and esteems, one thereby awakens others;

thus it is named a *pakṣa*. A *pakṣa* possesses both a basis (*āśraya*) and an essence (*svabhāva*). The "subject" (*dharmin*) that is universally established and is presented first is the basis of the *pakṣa*.

The "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is universally established; it refers to the subject (*pakṣa*) as the essence of the thesis. Because it is that upon which the essence of the thesis depends, it is called the "basis of the thesis" (*pakṣāśraya*).

When the essence of the thesis serves as the qualifier, then the basis of the thesis becomes the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Regarding the term "dharma-possessor" (*dharmin*): for example, [qualities such as] form (*rūpa*) or sound (*śabda*), because they possess an objective reality that accords with the mind, they are called "dharma-possessors.
Regarding the term "universally established" (*prasiddha*): these qualifiers and the qualified must be established by both the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*).

When both parties agree, it is called "thoroughly established" (*prasiddha*). Question: Since the essence of a thesis (*pakṣa*) consists of that which is contested between the proponent and the opponent, why must there be mutual agreement for it to be thoroughly established?
Answer: At the very moment one opens one's mouth, the opponent may immediately object, saying, "In the world, such a principle does not exist at all;
why bother to debate? In this way, the proposed position fails to be established. Therefore, [the thesis] must first be silenced [of such objections].

The traces of dispute serve merely as the path for entering into dispute. For instance, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty established the *vijñaptimātra-pramāṇa* (the valid cognition of consciousness-only), stating:
"True and universally established form is the subject (*dharmin*).

This term 'universally established' excludes both types of form that are not universally established—namely, the defiled forms of the final-body Bodhisattvas as asserted by the various Hīnayāna schools, and all forms [asserted by] the Buddhas..."
Because the Mahāyāna does not admit the existence of contaminated (*sāsrava*) form (*rūpa*). As for this being a property of another system that one does not oneself accept:

if one were to establish it as "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), one would commit the fault of partial non-establishment of the specific object of proof (*viśeṣya-asiddhi*) for oneself, and also the fault of contradicting one's own tenet (*siddhānta-virodha*).
This is because the Mahāyāna tenet asserts the form of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the uncontaminated form (*anāsrava-rūpa*) of the Buddhas, whereas the Hīnayāna does not.

Because it is accepted [by us]. This is something that, while being our own doctrine, is not accepted by the opponent. If one were to establish it as "mere consciousness" (vijñaptimātra), one would commit the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the qualified object (*viśeṣya-asiddhi*) for one part of the opponent.
Furthermore, both of these two reasons suffer from the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the substratum (*āśraya-asiddhi*) for one part of either [the subject or the predicate].
The term "universally established" (*prasiddha*) is used to exclude such cases; here, we establish two [reasons] that are mutually accepted by both parties.

Since all forms (*rūpa*) are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), the latter member of the thesis statement—that they are certainly not separate from visual consciousness—is an established qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Question: Since the Hīnayāna schools do not admit that form is not separate from visual consciousness, why does this not incur the fault of the qualifier being unestablished (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*)?
Answer: This is the locus of the thesis (*dharmin*) for the present argument; however, within the system of the opponent's school, there exists the sense of "not being separate."

This is indeed established. For the Hīnayāna school admits that when visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) takes a form (*rūpa*) as its object, it directly grasps its essence in a manner that is not separate from it;

furthermore, they admit that the very substance of the visual consciousness itself is likewise not separate from the visual consciousness. Therefore, there is no fault of the distinguishing factor being unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Question:

Since both parties agree that [the object] exists, how can there not be the fault of "conformity" (*sādhya-sama*)? Answer: In the Mahāyāna, it is merely accepted that the object is not separate from the mind;

there is no real external object. If the subject and predicate are combined to form the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the proponent accepts this while the opponent does not, and the proponent and opponent thus dispute over it, this is called the essence of the thesis (*pakṣa-svarūpa*). Therefore, there is no fault of conformity. In this context...
This is merely a verbal dispute; the underlying intention has not yet been examined. Regarding the phrase "because of their distinct natures":

this refers to the fact that upon the basis (*āśraya*) and the essence (*svabhāva*) of the thesis (*pakṣa*), there exist these various distinct natures. Therefore, it is absolutely necessary to employ the term "universally established" (*prasiddha*) to differentiate them;
only then will one avoid the five fallacies of contradiction within a pseudo-thesis (*pratijñābhāsa*) and the four [fallacies] of non-establishment (*aprasiddha*).

This is an error. The three phrases concerning "following one's own pleasure" have already been explained previously. That which can be established by means of a reason is called the "probandum" (*sādhya*).
For example, "sound is impermanent" is the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣa*). Regarding the nine types of reasons (*hetu*), all take "sound" as the factual entity (*dharmin*);
the essence of sound is subtle and does not fall within the category of the four atoms (*paramāṇu*). As for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in relation to the four atoms...
There are those that possess [the characteristics] and those that do not; only sound possesses them all. Therefore, some calculate it to be permanent, while others calculate it to be impermanent.

Now, both permanence and impermanence are extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Yet, this [treatise] establishes impermanence as its primary thesis, only to repeatedly cite the thesis of permanence when pointing out faults later on.
This surely has a deliberate intent. The state of permanence is superior and is what sentient beings delight in; thus, many develop an attachment to it.
[The mark of] attachment is inferior; it is impermanent, capable of inducing all forms of suffering, and easily gives rise to weary detachment.

For this reason, the sūtras and śāstras extensively refute the view of permanence and repeatedly speak of impermanence. To understand this meaning is to have completed more than half the contemplation of this treatise.
Part Two: The Causes (four sections). First, the general presentation of the three characteristics.

The reason (*hetu*) has three characteristics. What are these three? They are: (1) being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), (2) being necessarily present in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and (3) being entirely absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).

The *Huayan chao* states: "That which is called the 'reason' refers to the meaning and characteristic of that by which [a conclusion] is derived, the ground for it, its conformity and benefit, and its dependence."
It is thus. Because there is this basis, this reason for conformity, benefit, and dependence, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and its result (*phala*) can only be clarified.
Therefore, these are called "reasons" (*hetu*). This is precisely what the thesis depends upon, as well as the grounds by which the thesis is established.
By means of this, it is revealed that [the reason] is of one and the same flavor with the thesis to be established; being able to establish the thesis is what is meant by [the term "reason"].
This refers to the cause (*hetu*). This cause encompasses both arising (*janman*) and realization (*bodha*). Each of these—arising and realization—has three types, as previously explained.

According to the discourse on wisdom and awakening, the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-anumāna*) penetrates the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and takes refutation and establishment as its primary aim.

Since it is stated that the essence consists of generating wisdom and realizing [the truth], the two causes of arising and realization each take the first of the three types as their cause; this is made clear.
The two chapters on "Similarity" and "Difference" will be explained below. The *dharmas of the thesis* (*pakṣadharma*) are the reason (*hetu*).

To establish such a thesis by means of such a reason is called the "dharma of the thesis. Alternatively, it is said: when one utters the word "sound," before the thesis has been established, that which expresses the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of sound is termed the "property-possessor" (*dharmin*).
If one says, "it is impermanent," this then expresses a specific attribute (*viśeṣa*) of sound.
That is to say, it is the sound that is impermanent; it is not permanent. What is now called the "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*) refers to a specific property.
Within this context, the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) are names established for each individual reason (*hetu*) in relation to the three loci (*tatra*).

For example, when establishing that "sound is impermanent because it is produced," the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is like a pot, and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is like space and so forth. This very [point]...

The property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) exists determinately upon the subject, the sound that is impermanent; this is called "the property of being present in the entire subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*).
It exists determinately upon similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar; this is called "the property of being necessarily present in similar instances" (*sapakṣe sattvam*).

When one observes that the "produced nature" (kṛtakatva) is entirely absent from heterogeneous instances (*vipakṣa*), such as space and other dissimilar phenomena, this is called its "pervasive absence in heterogeneous instances.
Only when this produced nature possesses these three characteristics does it truly constitute a valid reason for impermanence.
These three characteristics reverse the fourteen fallacies of pseudo-reasons mentioned below. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the two [remaining] characteristics.

What are called the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)? The category of objects that share the same meaning as the property to be established is called the similar instance.

For example, when establishing impermanence, things such as a jar, which are impermanent, are called the similar instance. As for the dissimilar instance, it refers to those cases where the property to be established is absent;
for example, if something were permanent, one would observe that it is not produced, such as space and so forth.

The "established phenomenon" (sādhyadharma) refers to the property of the thesis being established. This means that the example must be equivalent and equal in its essential category to the meaning of the thesis;
this is called the "similar instance" (sapakṣa). For example, when establishing impermanence, it is the phenomenon to be established. A jar and so forth are impermanent.
The term "equal" (*sādharmya*) refers to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). This location is the location of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

A dissimilar instance is defined as that which stands in opposition to the similar instance by being its direct antithesis in relation to the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). The single word "non-existent" (*abhāva*) does not merely signify contradiction or difference;
therefore, Nāgārjuna stated: "In this context, if an instance is proximate to and equal to the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*), it is called a similar instance."
Since all meanings are designated as the "similar class" (*sapakṣa*), that which is not established [as such] is called the "dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*).
It is neither contradictory to nor different from the similar class. If it were contradictory, there would be only exclusion; if it were merely different, there would be no logical reason (*hetu*).
By this principle, [the reason] "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) can establish [the properties of] impermanence, selflessness, and so forth. It does not [establish them] by contradiction.

Because it is contradictory. If a property (*dharma*) can establish what is contradictory to that which is to be proven, this is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha-doṣa*), and it is termed a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*).
Just as with non-contradictory properties, so too is it with contradictory ones; for the property to be proven lacks both certainty and existence.

It is not like the case of a jar or similar things where the reason leads to doubt, because in those cases there is no mutual presence (*anvaya*) among them. This is because the nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is directly perceived.
The absence of a pot exists in relation to cloth and other things, whereas the absence of impermanence does not exist in relation to non-self and so forth;
since this reason [of presence] applies here, how can one distinct phenomenon occur in another location? Because they are similar, it is not stated by a different name that "this is precisely that."
Therefore, there is no fault. If one does not state that [the reason] is distinct, how can this reason be called a "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*)?

Here, it is merely stated that it is definitely a property of the thesis; it is not intended to say that it is *only* a property of the thesis. If that were the case, then the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) would also have to be called the thesis.
This is not so, because the thing to be proven (*sādhya*) is stated separately. Thus, the reason must be non-distinct [from the subject] for inference (*anumāna*) to be established. Therefore...
They are not similar. △ Third, the conclusion establishing the nature of the reason (*hetu*).

Herein, the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*)—or the property of being originated by immediate and uninterrupted effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*)—is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in its entirety;
it is definitely present in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and entirely absent from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). This constitutes the reason for [the property of] impermanence and so forth.
The preceding explanation of the two categories—the similar and the dissimilar—did not yet clarify the nature of the reason (*hetu*).

It is only here that the three natures of the reason are summarized and demonstrated. For example, when the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is adduced, this reason must possess these three natures to be a valid reason for impermanence.
Regarding "pervading the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*): it means that whatever is of the nature of being produced is necessarily impermanent.

Regarding the rule of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*): if there is even the slightest deviation from this rule of the thesis, then the reason (*hetu*) becomes the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*).

As for "being definitely present in the similar class" (*sapakṣe sattvam eva*): this property of being produced must definitely exist within the phenomena that constitute the similar class—namely, impermanent things—in order to function as a valid reason.
Even if it were not definitely present among the phenomena of the similar class, [it would fail to be a valid reason].
The fallacy of the "uncertainty of the thesis" (*sādhya-sama*) is equivalent to the "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*). Regarding "universal absence in the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣe 'tyantābhāva*):

this property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) must be entirely absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), such as space (*ākāśa*). If there were even a slight degree of being produced within the dissimilar class, this reason would be too broad (*vyabhicāra*), resulting in a contradictory uncertainty (*viruddhānaikāntika*).
Therefore, these three essential properties (*trairūpya*) reverse the fourteen fallacies. (From the *Nyāyamukha*).
The treatise discusses nine types of *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject). These are: establishing that sound is eternal because it is an object of cognition;
or establishing it as impermanent because it is produced; or establishing it as produced immediately following volitional effort because it is impermanent;

or establishing it as eternal because it is produced; or establishing it as eternal because it is audible; or establishing it as eternal because it [is produced] immediately following volitional effort...
Because it is produced by a specific nature; or because it is not produced by uninterrupted effort (*abhiyoga*), due to its impermanence;
or one establishes it as impermanent because it is produced by uninterrupted effort; or one establishes it as permanent because it is intangible (*apratigha*).

Within this, the propositions (*pakṣa*) and reasons (*hetu*) formulated to expose fallacies do not exceed these nine types. This is established as a formal determination based on what is produced (*kṛtaka*).
The nature of being produced by effort applied without interval is a correct reason for impermanence, as it fulfills the three characteristics of a valid reason.
While the nature of being produced [by causes] may be so, the nature of being produced by effort applied without interval is not a correct reason even for the thesis of impermanence.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: "As previously established, sound is impermanent; [produced by] effort applied without interval..."
Because it is produced by effort; for we observe that what is produced by uninterrupted exertion either manifests or arises.
Thus, doubt arises as to whether that which is now being established manifests or arises. Therefore, one should not use such a reason to prove the meaning of impermanence.
Furthermore, the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—such as lightning and the like, as well as the sound of a tree—is not produced by uninterrupted exertion.
The sounds of water and wind are likewise impermanent; thus, they are not universally non-existent. Furthermore, this would lack the third characteristic [of a valid reason].

This is merely cited by way of illustration. It is an error to claim that among many causes, these two causes are identified as the nature of the "proving cause" (*sādhana-hetu*) within this treatise.
The Master of the Treatise cites this for the sake of easy understanding. Now, one should...
Taking Master Xuanzang’s inference as the formal standard: the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that the aforementioned form is not separate from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). The reason (*hetu*) is:
"Because it is admitted [by you] to be included within the first three [bases], yet it is not included among the eyes. The concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like visual consciousness.

Within the thesis, "visual consciousness" is intended to mean the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), which is the consciousness as cause; within the example, "visual consciousness" is intended to mean the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*), which is the consciousness as effect and aspect.

Since the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is never separate from the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), the intention of the Tripiṭaka Master is to accept the objective aspect as a *dharmin* (the subject of the proposition).
If this is so, why not formulate the following formal inference (*pramāṇa*)? **Thesis:** The objective aspect is a *dharmin* that is certainly not separate from the self-verifying aspect.

**Reason:** Because it is a constituent part of that consciousness. **Homologous Example:** Just like the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*). [The opponent] says: "This is the [view of] the Hīnayāna..."
Because it is not permitted for there to be four parts, and fearing the commission of faults such as "conformity" (*anuvartana*) and so forth, one simply speaks of "eye-consciousness. Question:

When this measure is expressed in words, what kind of form (*rūpa*) is established? Answer: If one considers only the verbal expression, then neither the "characteristic aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*) nor the "substantial aspect" (*dravya-bhāga*) can be established.
However, if one aligns the mind with the expression, then the characteristic aspect-form is established. Since the characteristic aspect has been divided...

To divide the essence of matter (*rūpa*) would be something not universally established (*aprasiddha*). Regarding the first part of the statement, why do you say it refers to "universally established matter"? Because the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not commonly accepted [by both parties]. It is said:

If one considers the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) as presented in the statement, then since "matter" is accepted by both the proponent and the opponent, the term "universally established" is attached.

However, if it refers to the matter of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga-rūpa*), this is merely what is intended within the Mahāyāna; how could it concern the specific characteristic presented in the statement? How could it possibly...

Is this not universally established? Regarding the statement "included within the first three," among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), one takes the first element from each of the three groups of six;
these are the eye faculty element (*cakṣur-indriya-dhātu*), the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*), and the visible-form object element (*rūpa-viṣaya-dhātu*).
These are the first three elements among the eighteen. Even if one did not say "included within the first three," but simply said "not included by the eye," there would still be [others].

What is the fault? It is said: there are two faults. First, the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); second, the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (*svaśāstravirodha*). Regarding the fault of being inconclusive:

if one were to formulate the syllogism as follows—"That which is truly established color is necessarily not separate from eye-consciousness (the self-cognizing aspect)," with the reason: "because... [it would be inconclusive].
Because it is not subsumed by the eye, it is like the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

Thus, the reason—that it is not subsumed by the eye—is too broad (*asādhāraṇa*), as it applies to the five subsequent [consciousnesses] and the three [mental factors] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), all of which are likewise not subsumed by the eye. Consequently, the opponent points out the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), stating:

"Is it not the case that, just as the seeing-portion of visual consciousness is not subsumed by the eye, yet the seeing-portion of visual consciousness is not separate from visual consciousness itself?"

[The self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) asks: Does it not establish that the color-form universally accepted [by you] is not separate from the eye-consciousness [as its self-cognizing aspect]?

Or is it like the last three [faculties] among the five, which are also not subsumed by the eye? Are the last three definitely separate from the "seeing aspect" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eye-consciousness, while you instead establish that the color-form universally accepted by you is definitely separate from the eye-consciousness [as its self-cognizing aspect]?
Question: Now, the Mahāyāna states that the last three [faculties] among the five are also not separate from the eye.

[Question]: Is it possible [for the subsequent five consciousnesses] to obtain the visual aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)? [Answer]: Even if the Mahāyāna were to grant that the latter five consciousnesses also do not depart from the visual aspect of eye-consciousness, one would still incur the fault of an indeterminate [reason].
This would contradict one's own school’s tenet, for the Mahāyāna school asserts that the latter five consciousnesses definitely depart from the visual aspect of eye-consciousness.
Therefore, the inclusion of "the first three" as a partial cause is established to exclude the possibility that the latter five consciousnesses are included within the first three. [Question]: But...
If one says [the reason] is "subsumed under the first three [bases]" but does not say it is "not subsumed by the faculties," what fault is there? Answer: There are two faults:

first, the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); second, the fault of contradicting the determined specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon itself. Regarding the inconclusive: if one were to formulate a syllogism as follows:

"The color established as real is certainly not separate from the eye-consciousness (its self-cognizing part)," and the reason is "because it is subsumed under the first three [bases]," [the reason would be inconclusive].

For example, it is like the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*). Since this is subsumed under the first three [categories] and its cause is broad, one turns toward a dissimilar example regarding the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and raises an indeterminate objection:

"Is it the case that, just as the seeing-portion of visual consciousness is subsumed under the first three [categories], and the seeing-portion of visual consciousness is not separate from the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of visual consciousness, so too is the proven color-form (*rūpa*) not separate from the self-cognizing portion of visual consciousness? Or is it the case that the eye-faculty is also [subsumed under] the first three?"

[Included in the] Compendium. Is it not established for you that the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is not necessarily inseparable from the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) [in its aspect of seeing], just as it is established that form (*rūpa*) is not necessarily inseparable from the eye-consciousness [in its aspect of self-cognition]?
Question: Why do you not say "necessarily separate," but rather "not necessarily inseparable"? Answer:

From the perspective of the Mahāyāna, the eye-faculty, in relation to the eye-consciousness [in its aspect of seeing], is neither necessarily identical nor necessarily separate. Furthermore, regarding why it is not separate: the faculty is the cause of consciousness.

The *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) is the fruit. Because they are simultaneous, they are not identical; yet because matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—as their respective *darśana-bhāgas*—are distinct, it is simply said that they are "not definitely separate.

Regarding the second fault, the contradiction with the determined intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the dharma: the opponent presents a syllogism of contradiction as follows: "Visible form, as established by common consensus, is the subject (*dharmin*).
It is not the case that it is not inseparable from visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*); this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: first..."

Because of the three types of inclusion, it is like the sense organ of the eye. That is, the opponent takes the previous dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and takes the similar instance as a dissimilar instance.
Question: Does this result in establishing a contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property to be proven? Answer: This is not a genuine refutation.

Now, regarding the logical reason (*hetu*) that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*) to be proven: it must be established such that for the proponent, both [the similar instance and the dissimilar instance] are absent, while for the opponent, both are present;

only then does it constitute a contradiction of the specific characteristic of the property. In the present case, both the proponent and the opponent agree that the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) exists and that the boundary-instance (*avadhāraṇa-dṛṣṭānta*) exists.

Therefore, this is not a genuine fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic of the property. Question: What is the purpose of the phrase "admitted by oneself" (*svayam-abhyupagama*) at the beginning of the reason?

Answer: Within the scope of the three baskets (*piṭaka*), there is the fallacy of contradiction regarding the specific characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) in the context of transgressions.

In the method of logic (*hetuvidyā*), if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possesses such a fault, one admits the use of the phrase "admitted by oneself" (*abhyupagata*) as a refutation. Since the means of valid cognition within the three baskets currently possesses this fault, the phrase "admitted by oneself" is placed [in the syllogism] as a refutation.
Question: How can such a fault exist? Answer: Because, according to the Mahāyāna school, there are two kinds of form (*rūpa*). There is...
Apart from the color that is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of eye-consciousness, there exists color that is not apart from the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of eye-consciousness.

If one were to posit color apart from eye-consciousness, the Hīnayāna would grant such a claim; however, if one posits color that is not apart from eye-consciousness, the Hīnayāna does not grant it. Now, the Tripiṭaka Master states:

According to the ultimate truth, "color as a real entity" (*dharmī*) is that which is established through consensus. If one considers it in terms of the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) expressed by words, this is color admitted by both the proponent and the opponent;

and when citing the reason—that it is included within the first three [elements] but not included within the eye—it merely establishes that the commonly accepted color is not separate from visual consciousness.
If, however, one considers what is intended by the Tripiṭaka masters, it merely establishes that the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) of color is not separate [from consciousness].
Visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) takes as its logical subject (*dharmin*) that which is subsumed under the first three [categories] but not subsumed by the eye;

therefore, it posits a distinct aspect of form (*rūpa*) as intended by the mind upon this subject. Consequently, it is certain that this form is not separate from visual consciousness. Thus, the ancient commentary states:

"That which is truly established as form is the self-characteristic of the subject (*dharmin*) (the *pūrvapakṣa*, the locus of the thesis); that form which is certainly not separate from visual consciousness is the self-characteristic of the property (*dharma*) (the *uttarapakṣa*)."

[The thesis is] "the essence of the school (*siddhānta*)". [The reason is] "it is definitely separate from the color of visual consciousness" (referring to *svabhāva-rūpa*). [The example is] "it is not the case that it is definitely separate from the color of visual consciousness" (referring to *nimitta-bhāga-rūpa*);

this is the qualification of the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣa*, i.e., the qualification of the *pūrvapakṣa*). The proponent intends (*abhyupagata*) that it is not separate from the color of visual consciousness (referring to the *nimitta-bhāga*). Question:

When the opponent points out the fallacy of contradiction with the subject (*dharmibādha*) regarding the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) of the Tripiṭaka, how can the phrase "intends" (*abhyupagata*) serve as a defense? Answer: [It does so by showing that the opponent's charge fails because they themselves accept the proponent's intended meaning.]

When the opponent presents a counter-inference (*viruddhānumāna*), one uses the two words "self-admitted" (*svīkṛta*) to point out the fallacy of the opponent's reason being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Since the opponent's inference already carries this internal fallacy, what further logic could possibly reveal the fallacy of the subject's contradictory attributes (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha*) within the Tripitaka’s own inference?
Question: What is the formal structure (*ākāra*) of the counter-inference presented by the Hīnayāna? Answer: The Hīnayāna...
It is said: At first glance, the stated words appear to be free from fault in their three members (*trirūpa*), yet upon investigating what is actually established, it is fundamentally implicit.

If one intends to establish—upon the *dharmin* (the subject)—that the "intended" aspect of form (*nimittabhāga-rūpa*) is not separate from eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) (this being the thesis intended by the proponent), then the "seeing" aspect of eye-consciousness (*darśanabhāga*) [would be undermined].

It can serve as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). For example, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is never separate from visible form (*rūpa*), because all visible forms are indeed separate from visual consciousness.
Since they are separate from visual consciousness, they cannot serve as a similar instance; they thus become a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

Consequently, the initial reasons, such as "the first three," instead apply to the dissimilar instance—the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*)—and, without altering the proponent’s reason, establish a contradictory inference (*viruddha-pramāṇa*).

(Applying the same [formula] for the one existent dharma, it is said: "Because it is truly established as form (*rūpa*) [the subject of the thesis]; it is not the case that it is not inseparable from visual consciousness" [this is the intended meaning of the proponent regarding the subject of the thesis, and the reason is not altered].

"It is included in the first three [elements] and is not included among the eyes" [reversing the difference to establish a similarity]. The similar example is "like the visual faculty. To state the application:
whatever is included in the first three [elements] and is not included among the eyes is not not inseparable from visual consciousness.
The similar example (*sapakṣa*) is like the eye-faculty; the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) is like the eye-consciousness. This does not mean that [the object] is non-existent.

For there is no [object] that is not distinct from the eye-consciousness and its form. This immediately refutes the intention of the Tripiṭaka Master, who maintains that the *bhāga* (part) of form is non-existent.

Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master intentionally included the phrase "as he himself admits" (*svayaṃmata*) to take the forms of Buddhas in other directions and thereby establish the fallacy of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) for the opponent's formal inference (*bāhyamāna*). Thus, he exposes their error.
[The opponent] says: "Is it not like the case where visual consciousness is included within the first three [bases] but is not subsumed by the eye?
Does this not prove that, according to your own established tenet, form is not separate from visual consciousness? [The respondent asks:

"Is it not like my own admission that the form of Buddhas in other directions is also included within the first three [bases] but is not subsumed by the eye? Is the form of Buddhas in other directions not..."

If one excludes color from visual consciousness and yet seeks to prove that the color established by you is not excluded from visual consciousness, the opponent’s formal argument (*prayoga*) commits the fallacy of the "uncertainty of another" (*anyatarānyatara-asiddha*) within the common ground (*sādhāraṇa*). It is clear, therefore, that this is not a genuine refutation;

rather, the Tripiṭaka-master’s formal argument becomes a genuine proof (*sādhana*). If the reason (*hetu*) does not state "as admitted by oneself," it would be in vain to bring forward the Buddha of another direction.
The argument that "form" (*rūpa*) contradicts the external opponent’s means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) commits the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is not accepted by the other [party], namely the Śrāvaka. Thus, one incurs the fallacy of being "unestablished for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*).

This is because the opponent does not accept this specific factor—that the form of a Buddha in the first three realms is included within the category of "not apprehended by the eye" among the reasons cited. △ Third, the two analogies. First, the enumeration.
There are two kinds of analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*): first, the analogy of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*);
second, the analogy of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). In full, it is called *pī-yù* (譬喻). "Pì" (譬) means to compare; "yù" (喻) means to clarify.

That is to say, by comparing [the subject] with a proximate matter, one causes [the listener] to attain clear understanding of the profound Dharma. As Asaṅga says: "An analogy is that which shows the meaning of a particular aspect," meaning that by means of a perceived aspect...
That which is a correct statement regarding an aspect not yet seen [by the opponent] is called an analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Siṃhabuddhi says:
"The 'aspect already seen' refers to the portion that has been made manifest; the 'aspect not yet seen' refers to the portion not yet made manifest.

Because within the concordant example (*sapakṣa*), it is not necessarily the case that the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) and the meaning of the thesis are similar. This...

Furthermore, because other examples would themselves require establishment by further examples, this would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, it is not necessarily the case that all categories exist;
