"If the reason were merely the probandum itself, or if it were of a similar class with its specific distinctions, then the examples would be infinite, as well as [the requirement for] exclusion."

Regarding the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*): in the world, one merely employs a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to show that the reason (*hetu*) exists in a location other than that of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

It does not mean that the reason lacks existence in a place where the thesis is absent; therefore, [the mere presence of the reason in the similar instance] certainly lacks probative power. If the nature of being a reason consisted solely in its being a property of the thesis, [it would be fallacious].
If there were uncertainty, it would also constitute a valid reason (*hetu*).

How could there be such a fault when both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), along with two types of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding the property of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣadharma*), are fully present?

Such a fault occurs only at that time when the dissimilar instances of the probandum are not of a single type—namely, as in the first and the last three [reasons], where each has its final example. Therefore, the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) are established exclusively [as necessary].

To clarify the reason: by this principle, although all parts are capable of serving as the reason (*hetu*) to manifest what is to be established (*sādhya*), only one part is for the time being designated as the reason.
△ Second, the citation and explanation has two sections. First, the similar example (*sapakṣa*).

The "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is that wherein it is demonstrated that the reason is invariably present; that is to say, if something is produced, it is seen to be impermanent, as in the case of a jar and the like.

"This locus" refers to the locus of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). To "reveal that the reason coexists with the similar instances" means that when establishing a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one must first demonstrate that this example is conjoined with the similar instances of the previously stated reason, thereby showing that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—in this case, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—necessarily exists therein. Only then should one conjoin it with the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) to be established;

in this way, there will be no fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha-hetu*). Furthermore, by subsequently conjoining it with the thesis to be established, there will be no fault of the thesis being unestablished (*asiddha-sādhya*).

The fallacies of establishing [the reason] alone, the consequence [alone], or both failing to be established. This refers to the following: the citation of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Within this, the first eight characters constitute the synthesis (*upanaya*) of the reason followed by the thesis (*pratijñā*).
In this way, there are no fallacies of non-synthesis (*anupanaya*) or inverted synthesis (*viparītopanaya*).

"Just as a jar, etc. is the formal presentation of the body of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-vastu*). An example consists of both a locus (*āśraya*) and an entity (*vastu*). Jars and so forth are the loci of the example; each...
The nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the喻體 (*dārṣṭāntika*, the property to be illustrated). Now, we take the喻體 and do not take the喻依 (*dṛṣṭānta*, the locus of the illustration).
One should not differentiate between sound and a jar as being distinct; rather, one takes only the similarity in the sense of impermanence as the reason (*hetu*).
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: "There are three kinds of similarity in being produced. If one objects that the nature of being produced, such as that of a jar, does not exist in sound..."
It appears to be unestablished (*asiddha*). If one objects that the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) does not exist in a pot and so forth, this is a pseudo-contradiction (*viruddhābhāsa*).

If one objects that it likewise does not exist in that very same [subject] when it is eternal, this is a pseudo-indeterminate (*anaikāntikābhāsa*) because it is an uncommon [reason] (*asādhāraṇa*), or it is a pseudo-fault of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣābhāsa*) because it cites a similar instance (*sādharmya*).
Why is this? Because inference (*anumāna*) is established by taking only the general property (*sāmānyadharma*), and not by taking the particular (*viśeṣa*). If...

Because they are determined to be distinct in their specific meanings, inference would otherwise be impossible. What is called the "universal property" (sāmānyadharma) is the essence of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

What is called the "specific meaning" (viśeṣārtha) is the locus of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*). If anything is deficient, it constitutes the fallacy of a pseudo-homologous example (*sādharmyadṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
Next, the four types of heterologous examples (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*): first, the formal presentation of the heterologous example.
The dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is as follows: where it is stated that the probandum is absent, the reason is entirely non-existent;
for example: "If something were eternal, it would be seen to be unproduced, such as space and so forth."

"This locus" refers to the locus of the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*). "Stating that the probandum is absent" means that the previously established thesis (*pakṣa*) of impermanence does not exist within this dissimilar example;
thus, there is no fault of contradicting the probandum. "The reason is entirely non-existent" means...
This means that the reason (hetu), which was previously established as being necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), must be entirely absent from these dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

If this were not the case, there would be the fallacies of "the probans not being excluded" (*apradarśita-vyatireka*) and "both [probandum and probans] not being excluded" (*ubhayāpradarśita-vyatireka*).

For example, if one first excludes the thesis by saying, "If it were eternal," and subsequently excludes the reason by saying, "It is seen to be non-produced"—if this were done, there would be no avoidance of the two aforementioned fallacies, just as in the case of empty space.

"Space, etc."—this correctly presents the actual subject of the analogy. If there were any deficiency here, it would constitute the fallacy of a pseudo-contrastive example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
The sequence of the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) differs from that of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*), making the underlying logic difficult to comprehend.

If one argues that in the method of inference (*anumāna*), the thesis depends upon the reason for its clarification, and therefore the application first joins with the reason while the thesis follows accordingly, then why should the conclusion (*nigamana*) alone not be treated in the same way?

This merely presents the reason (*hetu*) to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*), cites the principle (*dharma*), and provides the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). It distinguishes the dissimilar and establishes the similar;
such is the force of the argument. For instance, the synthesis (*upanaya*) states: "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, as in the case of a jar. The separation (*vyatireka*) states:
"If it were permanent, it would be seen not to be produced, as in the case of space. How, then, is one to know that the nature of being produced establishes impermanence?
[The opponent] says: "I observe that all things which are produced are impermanent, just as the case with jars and the like" (this is the *upanaya*, or application).
"How can this reason (*hetu*) fail to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*) of permanence? [The proponent] replies:

"If something were permanent, it would not be produced, just as the case with space and the like" (this is the *apadeśa*, or exclusion). Thus, the words of the application follow the reason and precede the thesis.

Correct. To depart from the phrasing where the thesis (*pakṣa*) comes first and the reason (*hetu*) follows is correct; such is the natural order. Next, the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) is explained:

here, the term "permanent" indicates that which is not impermanent, and the phrase "not produced" indicates that which is not something produced—just as "non-existence" indicates that which is not existent.
It is termed "non-existent.

Regarding the explanation of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), it says: "That is to say, in this place, that which is to be established (*sādhya*) is absent. Regarding the explanation of the dissimilar property (*vyatireka*), it says:
"If, in this place, the absence of that which is to be established is stated, its nature as a universal non-existence is more than clearly elucidated. Fearing that people might still...

Because they are established as distinct through mutual exclusion, after the term "separation" (*viyoga*), it is further clarified that the permanent excludes the impermanent and the non-produced excludes the produced.
Thus, one perceives the difference between dissimilar phenomena;

this constitutes a difference based on the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), rather than a difference consisting of mutual exclusion or distinctness. Question: What is meant by "mutual exclusion and distinctness"?
"How does this differ from non-existence? He replied: "When two phenomena stand in opposition, one may speak of their contradiction or their distinctness.
Now, however, we are simply stating that this phenomenon is non-existent; how can there be no difference? It is like when 'non-being' is spoken of as 'non-being':
if there is a phenomenon, it is called 'non-existent' precisely because it lacks [existence]. How could there be a separate 'non-existence' that exists alongside existence?"

Contradiction and difference are distinct; how then can one claim they do not exist? That which is contradictory and different is termed "pseudo-similarity" (*sādharmya-sama*) and is not termed "difference" (*vaidharmya*).
This has already been fully cited from Nāgārjuna’s treatise above. △ Fourth, concluding that this constitutes a valid proof (*sādhana*).
The thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth—such multiple statements that bring about awakening in others when they are being explained—are termed "proof" (*sādhana*).

For example, the statement "Sound is impermanent" is the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavākya*). The statement "Because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmavākya*).

The statement "If something is produced, it is seen to be impermanent, like a jar and so forth" is the statement of the presence in similar instances (*sapakṣānvayavākya*). If, however, it is not seen in those [similar instances]... [the statement of absence in dissimilar instances].
To "act like space" is a term for being free from verbal expression. Only these three factors are called the "proof" (*sādhana*).

This precisely delimits the three members and establishes them as the proof. II. The Section on Fallacious Proofs (*sādhanābhāsa*). The first four [sections] concern fallacious theses (*pakṣābhāsa*); there are three types.
First, the general heading:
Although one may desire to establish [a thesis], because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, it is called a "pseudo-thesis" (*pratijñābhāsa*). That is to say:

contradiction with direct perception, contradiction with inference (*anumāna*), contradiction with one's own scriptures, contradiction with worldly consensus, contradiction with one's own words, and [contradiction] regarding the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The nine types of fallacious theses (*pakṣābhāsa*) consist of: [the thesis] being universally established; the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) not being universally established; both [the subject and the qualifier] not being universally established;

and being in contradiction with what is universally established. The five types of contradictory theses (*viruddha*) arise because the proposed thesis contradicts what is known through cognition, scripture, oneself, or others.
The four types of unestablished theses (*asiddha*) arise because the proponent and opponent do not accept the subject (*dharmin*), the predicate (*dharma*), or both.
Because it is perfectly established, both the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*) and the essence of the thesis (*pakṣasvabhāva*) are addressed together.

Some hold that being contradictory is a fault of the essence of the thesis, while being unestablished is a fault of the basis of the thesis; others hold that being contradictory is a fault of the basis of the thesis, while being unestablished is a fault of the essence of the thesis.
Both views are incorrect. II. Citation and Explanation (divided into two parts). First, the explanation of the five faults of contradiction.
Among these, that which contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is as follows: to say that "sound is not audible.

Since sound is the object of the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), which is a form of direct perception, one now establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) that "it is not audible" with respect to the subject (*dharmin*) that is sound.
Therefore, this contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for what contradicts this means of valid cognition: it is like asserting that jars and the like are permanent.
The conceptual cognition that apprehends jars, garments, and so forth is called inference (*anumāna*); thus, one establishes the thesis that jars and the like are permanent.
This constitutes a contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*).
Regarding contradiction with one’s own teaching (*sva-śāstra-viruddha*): for example, the Vaiśeṣika masters establish sound as eternal;
yet among the twenty-four qualities (*guṇa*) in the Vaiśeṣika system, sound is exclusively produced (*kṛtaka*), while the others are either produced or unproduced (*akṛtaka*).
Furthermore, it is claimed that there are three kinds of sound: first, those produced by conjunction; second, those produced by disjunction; and third, those produced by sound itself.

Now, whatever can be joined or separated, and whatever has arising and ceasing, shares the nature of being produced and is therefore impermanent. To establish such [sounds] as eternal contradicts one's own teaching.
Contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka-virodha*) is, for example, as when it is said that the hare-marked [rabbit] is not the moon because it does not exist there;
or as when it is said that human skull-bone is pure because it is a part of a sentient being, just like a conch shell.
There are two kinds of worlds: first, the world of those in training (*śaikṣa*); second, the world of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
It is commonly said in the mundane world that a rabbit becomes pregnant due to the moon; now, to say it is not due to the moon contradicts the world of those beyond training.
When practitioners of the Two Vehicles cultivate the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), they observe that there is nothing about the bodies of sentient beings that is not impure.
Now, to say that human skull-bone is pure contradicts worldly consensus regarding those who are still training (*śaikṣa*). Regarding the "Threefold Valid Cognition" (*tri-pramāṇa*), it states:
"Form is established as real. The two characters "real" (*tattvataḥ*) serve to exclude the fault of contradicting worldly consensus, as well as the fault of contradicting scripture and so forth.
An opponent asks: "The world universally knows that form exists apart from consciousness; how is it that the Mahāyāna now establishes form [as being identical to consciousness]?"

"It is not separate from eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), because that would contradict what is commonly known in the world. Why, then, does it not incur the fault of contradicting worldly consensus? Answer:

"In establishing an inference (*anumāna*), there are those that are autonomous (*svatantra*) and those that are for the sake of others (*parārtha*). Each, according to its application, has its own specific qualification.

If it is an autonomous inference (meaning one establishes a thesis for oneself to cause another to understand), it is qualified by the phrase 'admitted by oneself' (*abhyupagata*), which clarifies that the statement admitted by oneself is free from faults such as being contradicted by another [source]. If it is..."

In the case of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), when one presents a thesis (*pakṣa*) and reasons (*hetu*), the qualification "in reality" (*paramārthatas*) excludes faults such as contradicting one's own thesis.

In the case of common inference (*sāmānyānumāna*), when presenting an inference for others, the qualification "in reality" excludes faults such as contradicting one's own scriptures. Now, this common inference possesses a specific qualification:
the term "in reality" indicates that it is based upon the ultimate truth; specifically, it refers to the manifestation of essence and function among the four types of ultimate truths.
[The opponent] asserts: "It is not contradictory to worldly convention that what is not studied [by Mahāyāna practitioners] may be so.

Furthermore, as the World-Honored One permitted in the Hīnayāna Āgamas that form exists apart from consciousness, and since scholars of the Hīnayāna collectively reckon that there are real objects external to the mind, does this not contradict the teachings of the Āgamas and other texts for those Hīnayāna scholars? [The respondent] answers: "This is merely based on the Mahāyāna."
Establishing [the definition] according to the superior sense does not contradict the teachings of the Śrāvaka-vehicle, nor is it a worldly error.
Thus, one should know that if one establishes [it] solely by relying on the superior sense, then even if it contradicts worldly convention, it is not a fault.
Therefore, I have composed this to serve as a standard.
Regarding "contradiction with one's own words": it is like saying, "My mother is a barren woman.
To call her one's mother because she gave birth to one's body is to name her "mother"; yet a barren woman does not give birth.
To say that one's mother is a barren woman is a contradiction of one's own words. 2. Explanation of the four faults of non-establishment (*aprasiddha*).
Regarding the case where the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not established: for example, when a follower of the Buddha posits the destruction of sound against a Sāṃkhya.
The "qualifier" refers to the nature of the predicate (*pakṣa*), which is called "established" (*prasiddha*) because both the proponent and the opponent agree that this property exists.
Since the Sāṃkhya does not accept the destruction of sound, the nature of the qualified thesis (*viśeṣya-pakṣa*) is not established. According to [the treatise]:
In the *Treatise of Nāgārjuna*, the destruction of sound is established by means of the cause produced through diligent and uninterrupted effort.

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Refuting the Sense Bases and Objects" of the *Śataśāstra*, it is extensively argued that the subtle nature of sound disintegrates; this is specifically directed against the Sāṃkhya teachers who claim that [sound] is merely a conventional designation. This is incorrect.

Regarding "the subject [of the thesis] not being universally established": for example, when a Sāṃkhya teacher says to a Buddhist disciple, "The self (ātman) is volition," the "subject" (*dharmin*) presented in the first part of the statement is called the "subject of the thesis.
Because the Buddhist disciple does not accept the existence of a self, this subject—the basis of the thesis—is not universally established.

This is explained at length in the "Refutation of the Self" chapter (*Ātmapratiṣedha*) of the *Śataśāstra*, where the "self as volition" is extensively refuted; here, only that [particular aspect] is taken up.

The disciples of the Buddha do not admit the existence of a self (*ātman*), yet they do not deny volition (*cetanā*). This is because volition belongs to the category of universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*).

(In the *Śataśāstra*, this is a point of contention; the intention there is that while [the Buddha] admitted this, he spoke of it only as a conventional expression, which is why it differs [from our position]).

Regarding that which is not established for both parties: for example, when a Vaiśeṣika teacher, in debate with a Buddhist disciple, posits the "self" (ātman) as the synthesis that unites various conditions, neither [the existence of such a self nor its function] is established for either side.
The Vaiśeṣikas postulate six categories of existence (padārtha), the sixth of which is inherence (samavāya).
[The opponent] says: "As for 'conjunction' (*saṃyoga*): it is like a bird flying through the sky that suddenly lands on a tree branch and stays there without departing.

All distinct phenomena (*bhinnadharma*) suddenly conjoin; this is due to the nature of conjunction itself. [Response: A follower of the Buddha does not admit the existence of a "self" (*ātman*), as the object to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*) is not established.
Nor do we admit the existence of a "nature of conjunction," as the distinguishing attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not established.
Because it is not universally established, it is called "mutual non-establishment" (*ubhayāsiddha*).
Regarding "conformity with what is universally established" (*prasiddhasama*): for example, to say that sound is audible;
since both the proponent and the opponent agree that sound is audible, this is conformity, and this is universal establishment. Why is this also [considered a fallacy]?

[This is] a fault. For a proposition (*pakṣa*) is established as a fully proven principle (*prasiddha-dharma*) which, although accepted by both the proponent and the opponent, is understood as a thesis through the synthesis of the preceding and succeeding terms.
It is called the essence of the thesis when the proponent accepts it while the opponent does not, such that the proponent and opponent dispute over it.
If the opponent did not dispute it and the two parties were in agreement, how could the correct meaning be extended, and how could correct knowledge arise?
It arises; how could it not be a fault? △ Third, the conclusion establishing the fallacious thesis (*pratijñā-sadṛśa*):

These many words are so because they employ the method of negating the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, because they cannot be established, and because they result in no fruit (*phala*).
This is called the fallacy of a pseudo-thesis (*pratijñābhāsa*).
Because it negates the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, it constitutes the fifth fault among the contradictions.

For example, to say "sound is not audible" is a contradiction with the specific characteristic of sound, as the very expression "not audible" contradicts it. Likewise, to say "a jar is permanent" is... [and so forth].

This statement of permanence contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the jar and so forth; since it cannot be established, it incurs the four faults of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
The final phrase concludes that both sections fail to produce the fruit of knowledge. △ Second, pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): two [types].
First, the general heading:

Having already explained the fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), we shall now explain the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Those that are unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and contradictory (*viruddha*) are called fallacious reasons.

Wherever there is a deficiency in the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) of a reason, it is termed a fallacious reason. △ Second, the detailed explanation has three parts; first, the explanation [of the unestablished].
There are four types of non-establishment (*asiddha*).

First, the enumeration of their names: there are four types of non-establishment: first, non-establishment for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*); second, non-establishment for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*); third, non-establishment through doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*);
and fourth, non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
This [criticism] regards the reason (*hetu*) in light of the thesis (*pakṣa*). Furthermore, it is a case of "unestablished due to non-acceptance" (*asiddha-anabhyupagama*).

The commentator consequently considers this to be the fault of the "incomplete pervasion" (*avyāpti*) of the property of being a characteristic of the thesis (*pakṣadharma-tva*). Since it is already unestablished, how could one even discuss which aspect is deficient or by what aspect it is deficient?
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics.
For example, in establishing that sound is impermanent and so forth, if one were to say, "Because it has the nature of being visible to the eye," [the reason] would be unestablished for both parties.
This is the general statement; the subsequent reasons, such as "because it is a product" (*kṛtakatvāt*), are also to be understood by extension from this.
To take sound as the object of the eye is not only unacceptable to the opponent, but is difficult even for the proponent to maintain.

Because it is asserted by oneself, both [the proponent and the opponent] fail to establish it. Regarding these two characters, commentators generally take them to refer to the two positions of permanence and impermanence.
According to Nāgārjuna, that which is not accepted by both parties is certainly not a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*).
For example, if one were to establish that "sound is impermanent because it is visible to the eye," or if the opponent does not accept it, such as when debating with a Vaiśeṣika.
Regarding the reason "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*): it is understood that [the reason] is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent.
However, against the proponent of the Manifestation Theory (*abhivyaktivādin*), this reason is unestablished for at least one of the two parties.
It is acceptable to take "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) as the reason for impermanence.

However, with respect to the Śabdanityatvavādin (Proponent of the Manifestation of Sound), this commits the fallacy of the "unestablished for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*), because they do not admit that sound is produced.

Regarding the Śabdanityatvavādin, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Others are biasedly attached to the view that all sound is eternal; it is only through dependence on conditions for its manifestation that it is able to signify."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states: "The external Śabdika masters hold such a view and establish such a doctrine:
the characteristic of sound exists inherently, being neither produced nor extinguished; yet, it is only through repeated articulation that it becomes manifest, and the essence of sound is eternal."
When doubt arises regarding the nature of mist and the like, it is said that there exists a fire resulting from the combination of the great elements (*mahābhūta*);
yet, because of this hesitation, the [logical] proof is not established.
This is an illustration for one who posits a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) while holding a mistaken view. Seeing smoke from a distance, one infers the existence of fire.
What fault could there be? At present, regarding mist and the like, one has not yet ascertained whether it is smoke or not;
yet you have hastily established the verbal claim that fire exists as a combination of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). You should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:

That which is perceived as having such characteristics is the subject (*dharmin*)—namely, the nature of mist and so forth. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that fire exists as a combination of the primary elements. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because smoke is seen."
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are capable of producing [effects]; therefore, they are called "seeds.

Just as fire exists through the combination of fuel, charcoal, and so forth, and smoke is thereby produced, so too when doubt arises, it is precisely this state of hesitation. It is not necessary to divide the combination of the great elements into two distinct causes to constitute this hesitation.
Furthermore, the combination of the great elements constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*), not the reason (*hetu*), because smoke is actually perceived.
The *Treatise* by Nāgārjuna may be relied upon as the source.

Space is substantially existent because it is the substratum of qualities (*guṇa*). Against those who argue for the non-existence of space, the locus of the reason (*āśrayāsiddha*) would be unestablished.

Space is a real entity; "substantially existent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); the reason (*hetu*) is stated as "because it is the substratum of qualities. This is acceptable when stated from one's own perspective.
If one were to establish [the argument] against those who deny the existence of space (*ākāśa*), then the locus (*āśraya*) would be unestablished, because they do not admit that space exists.
Since space does not exist, what could the quality (*guṇa*) rely upon? Nāgārjuna said: "In some cases, the property (*dharma*) is unestablished."

Just as when establishing the self (*ātman*) as being omnipresent in essence because pleasure and so forth arise in all places, [the reason] is unestablished with respect to the proponent of non-self (*anātmavādin*).

Based on this, the "basis" (*āśraya*) is precisely the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*). If one asks, "How does this differ from [the fault of] the 'unestablishedness of the qualified' (*viśeṣyāsiddha*)?
[The answer is: The former refers to the unestablishedness of the thesis (*pakṣāsiddha*), whereas this refers to the unestablishedness of the reason (*hetvasiddha*). Therefore, it is not [the same].
The same. △ Second, the explanation of the uncertain [reasons] has two parts.

First, the listing of names. There are six types of uncertain reasons: first, the common; second, the uncommon; third, that which occurs in a portion of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) but pervades the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*);
fourth, that which occurs in a portion of the dissimilar class but pervades the similar class; fifth, that which occurs in a portion of both classes; and sixth, the contradictory certainty.
This uses an analogy to illustrate the "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) fallacy. Commentators alike regard the latter two reasons as having the fault of lacking the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

However, upon examining the intent of the treatise, it is precisely stated that the inconclusive refers to which school's position [is being refuted]; thus, it is merely missing the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
The "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) is precisely the cause of doubt. △ Second, the explanation of its characteristics:

Among these, the "common" (sādhāraṇa) is, for example, when one says, "Sound is eternal, because it is an object of cognition. In this case, both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal are common to this reason.
Therefore, it is inconclusive. For example, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), sound is impermanent, like a jar;
yet, because it is an object of cognition, sound is eternal, like space.

It is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) because two opposing tenets—eternal and non-eternal—share a single reason. As stated below: "Establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*): [Thesis: Sound is eternal; [Reason: Because it has the nature of being an object of cognition. This is the first of the nine types of *pakṣadharma*.

Herein, for the thesis of "eternal," "space" (*ākāśa*) serves as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). As for the phrase "To explain... and so forth: it sets forth the formal argument. The phrase "Eternal and non-eternal... and so forth: it analyzes the fallacy. The phrase "For example... and so forth: it explicitly presents the characteristics of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason.

Subsequent passages follow this pattern. [Formal Argument: Sound is eternal, because it has the nature of being an object of cognition. Among the nine types of *pakṣadharma*, this is the first type. In this context, regarding the thesis of "eternal," space is the similar instance.

The jar serves as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Since the reason (*hetu*) of "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) exists in both the similar and dissimilar instances, is sound a permanent effect or an impermanent one?
Therefore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding what is called "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*): for example, when it is said that sound is permanent because it possesses the nature of being audible, this reason is excluded from both the class of the permanent and the class of the impermanent.
Since nothing else exists outside of the permanent and the impermanent, this is a reason for doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*). To what, then, is this "nature of being audible" comparable?
The two positions of permanence and impermanence are both devoid of this reason; therefore, it is called "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).

To claim that sound is permanent because it possesses the property of being audible is the fifth of the nine types of fallacious reasons (*pakṣābhāsa*). This reason—being audible—takes emptiness (*ākāśa*) as its similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Since emptiness is not something that can be heard, how could it manifest permanence? Thus, the category of the permanent is devoid of this reason. As for the pot, it serves as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
In the chapter [on permanence], what is heard in the pot that manifests impermanence? If so, then the chapter on impermanence would also be devoid of this reason.
Since both locations are devoid [of it], and there is no phenomenon outside of these two, by what phenomenon should this nature of "being heard" be considered a similar instance (*sapakṣa*)?
This appears to lack the property of "necessarily existing in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*), but in fact, all three characteristics [of a valid reason] are deficient.
Regarding that which occurs in only a portion of the similar class while occurring throughout the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*):

for example, it is said that sound (the subject) is not produced by non-vigorous effort (the thesis), because it is impermanent (the reason). Herein, the thesis—that it is not produced by non-vigorous effort—is [present in] lightning and space...

These constitute its similar instances (sapakṣa). [Having first established the similar instances, the reason is now raised to expose the fallacy: This property of impermanence exists in part within lightning and so forth.

In [the locus of] space and so forth, [the reason] does not fail to occur in even a single part. It is not the case that it should not be absent and yet is absent, for that would contradict the property of being "certainly present in similar instances" (*sapakṣa*).

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is "not produced by immediate effort," taking jars and the like as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), because jars are produced immediately through human labor. [The reason] is present throughout those [dissimilar instances], because the entire substance of a jar is impermanent.
This would mean that the reason pervades the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), which it ought not to pervade; thus, it contradicts the requirement that it be entirely absent from the dissimilar class.

Since this reason takes both lightning and a jar as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*), it is also "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). [To explain the nature of inconclusiveness: Is it like a jar and so forth, because of having the nature of impermanence, such that it is produced through immediate effort?
Or is it like lightning and so forth, because of having the nature of impermanence, such that it is not produced through immediate effort?
(The cause for the indeterminate nature of the two destinies is not established).

Sound is of three kinds: first, that which has its cause in appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*), such as the sound of speech; second, that which has its cause in non-appropriated primary elements, such as the sound of trees;
third, that which has its cause in both [types of] primary elements, such as the sound of a hand and a drum (in which the hand is the appropriated element).
Because that which is grasped (upātta) is not [itself] grasped, it is said to be "both" (ubhaya). This sound is not produced by immediate effort;

rather, it is a sound whose cause consists of the ungrasped primary elements (mahābhūta). The sound produced below by immediate effort is a sound whose cause consists of both types of primary elements.
It is not produced by effort or without interruption, because it possesses the nature of impermanence. This is the seventh type among the nine kinds of *pakṣadharma* (subject-attributes).

Although these six subsequent phrases under "the nature of impermanence" correctly explain that [the reason] occurs in one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and occurs pervasively in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), they are in fact not words intended to state a formal logical fallacy;
rather, they merely serve to definitively establish lightning and a jar as the similar instances.

"Regarding the 'Dharma-ear' [example], the passage beginning with 'like a jar, etc. correctly sets forth the characteristic of being indeterminate (*anaikāntika*). The following two lines should also be understood accordingly.

That is to say, if one excludes a portion of non-pervasive emptiness and takes a pervasive jar as the subject of the property (*dharmin*), making it a common locus (*sādharmya*) with lightning, one may hope to avoid the fault of lacking two of the three characteristics; yet it remains indeterminate. Why? Because [the relationship between] lightning and the jar..."
Regarding these two things: if they reside within the cause of impermanence, they constitute "similar instances" (*sapakṣa*), because both of these things are impermanent.

However, within the thesis (*pakṣa*) of that which is not produced by non-continuous effort (*aprayatnāntarīyaka*), lightning is similar [to the subject] while a jar is dissimilar. Now, if one were to establish the thesis by citing the reason, there would be no certainty regarding the two categories.
Would one then establish the thesis of being produced by effort by means of an impermanent jar? Or else, by means of an [impermanent]...?

Is this not the doctrine that [lightning] is produced without effort? Since it is thus not established as a doctrine of production without effort, it does not possess the property of being a logical reason (pakṣadharma) that pervades the subject.
How could it be anything less than lacking both of the latter two characteristics [of a valid reason]? The subsequent items should be understood in this same manner.
That which occurs in one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) but occurs pervasively in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is as follows:

for example, when the thesis is established that "sound is produced immediately following volitional effort" (the thesis), because of its impermanent nature (the reason). Regarding the thesis of being produced immediately following volitional effort, things such as jars serve as the similar class (because they are likewise produced by volition).

As for this impermanent nature (this phrase governs the two subsequent instances of the character *yu*), it exists pervasively therein (which is precisely what is meant by "occurring pervasively in the similar class"). This [is not...]

[Lightning and space, etc., serve as] the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) because they are all not of the nature of being produced through effort. Among those, [the reason] exists in one part of them, such as lightning (this is precisely the fallacy of "presence in a portion of the dissimilar instance").
In others, such as space, it does not exist (this does not constitute a fallacy). Therefore, as before, this too is an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason.

Sound is produced by uninterrupted effort because it possesses the nature of impermanence. Among these nine types of *pakṣadharma* (reasons), this third type—like the previous one—is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is because the reason of impermanence, such as lightning and a jar, serves as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), yet [lightning] is not produced by uninterrupted effort.
Thus, it remains uncertain whether [sound] is like lightning, which is impermanent but not produced by uninterrupted effort.
Because [the subject] is impermanent like a jar and so forth, it is produced by effort and exertion;
this [reasoning] appears to lack the "pervasive absence in the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣāvyāvṛtti*), but in reality, all three characteristics are deficient.

Regarding "partial occurrence in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and one part [of the dissimilar class]": for example, it is said that "sound is permanent because it lacks material resistance" (this formulation of the syllogism will be analyzed for its fallacies below).

Here, the thesis (*pakṣa*) of permanence takes space (*ākāśa*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) as its similar class (since non-Buddhists consider atoms to be permanent, they are included in this similar class).

The property of lacking material resistance exists in space and so forth (because space lacks material resistance; thus, it occurs in only one part of the similar class), but it does not exist in atoms and so forth (because atoms possess material resistance).

Therefore, one part [of the reason] does not apply. This [part] should not be absent, yet it is absent). Taking the jar and pleasure (*sukha*) as the dissimilar instances (since both the jar and pleasure are impermanent), [the reason] applies to pleasure and so forth in that one part of being "without material obstruction" (this should not apply, yet it does apply).
In the case of the jar and so forth, it does not apply (since the jar possesses material obstruction, one part does not apply).
For this reason, because pleasure and space (*ākāśa*) are treated as similar instances, this reason is also called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

"Both" means that [the reason] occurs in one part of both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), while it does not occur in another part. For example: "Sound is eternal, because it lacks material resistance.
This is not included among the nine types of *pakṣadharma* (reasons). An explanation of this will be found later in the section on fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

In this case, the reason "lacking material resistance" does not occur in one part of the similar class, namely atoms (*paramāṇu*), yet it does occur in one part of the dissimilar class, such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. Therefore, it is a "both" [type].

One should exclude one portion—the non-transforming atoms—and take another portion—the transforming [atoms] such as pleasure (*sukha*)—to serve as the concordant instance (*sapakṣa*) alongside space (*ākāśa*).

However, this may be acceptable if the reason (*hetu*) is "lack of resistance" (*apratighāta*); yet, if the reason is advanced to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*), it becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For, will you establish that sound is eternal by means of space which lacks resistance, or will you... [lack of resistance]?
Is the pleasure that constitutes an obstruction impermanent? Regarding the character "pleasure" (*lè*): if it refers to the pleasure of music, then it is merely sound;
one cannot use sound as a metaphor for sound. It must be determined as the pleasure of sensation (*vedanā*).

This is because the Sāṃkhya masters maintain that the self (*ātman*) is consciousness (*cetanā*), which experiences the "great" (*mahat*) and other qualities produced by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The twenty-three factors are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. In older translations, these are rendered as "pleasure," "pain," and "delusion," and are also termed "joy," "sorrow," and "darkness.

In new translations, they are translated as "attachment" (*rāga*), "aversion" (*dveṣa*), and "delusion" (*moha*). For details, consult the *Saptati-śāstra* (Seventy Verses on Gold) and the *Śata-śāstra* (Extensive Hundred Verses).

Both treatises frequently discuss these three factors—pleasure and so forth—establishing formal syllogisms (*pramāṇa*) specifically to refute the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, they excel in identifying and defeating their most prominent leaders. Therefore...

The citation of examples, the citation of the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the citation of the reason (*hetu*) are all contained within these several types of argumentation; one should not provide further divergent explanations.
Regarding "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*): for example, one might establish a thesis by stating, "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced, like a jar."
Some establish that sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of being audible, just like the nature of sound itself.
Since both of these [reasons] are reasons of doubt, they are both termed "inconclusive" (anaikāntika).
"Sound is impermanent because it is a product. This is the second type among the nine kinds of propositions (*pakṣa*).

Alternatively, one might establish: "It is permanent because it is audible. This is the fifth type. In these cases, the proponent and opponent dispute over the same *dharmin* (the subject), yet the reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) differ for each;
the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) are complete, yet neither side is able to point out a flaw. For instance, even though the proponent [is unable to defeat the opponent] himself...
When one establishes impermanence, yet also admits that sound possesses the nature of being audible—sharing this same nature as sound—one cannot expose the fallacy of the thesis of permanence.

Although the opponent establishes permanence for themselves, they also admit that sound possesses the nature of being produced—sharing this same nature as a jar and so forth—and thus one cannot expose the fallacy of the thesis of impermanence. Since neither side can mutually expose the other's fallacy...
Both parties hesitate and are unable to establish a definitive school; consequently, they do not give rise to correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) regarding one another.

Therefore, this is called the "inconclusive fallacy of mutual contradiction" (*ubhayapakṣaikadeśavṛttiviruddhānaikāntika*). Commentators all claim that this [fallacy] lacks the third characteristic (*tṛtīyalakṣaṇa*); however, this is erroneous. △ Third, the explanation of contradiction has two parts.
First, the enumeration of names.

There are four types of contradiction: namely, the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the property (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the property (*dharma-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the locus (*dharmin-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), and the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the locus (*dharmin-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu*).

The *dharma* (predicate) refers to the *pakṣa-dharmatva* (the property of the subject) as stated in the latter member of the proposition. The *dharmin* (subject) refers to the basis of the *pakṣa* (the locus of the subject) as stated in the former member.

The "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) refers to the specific characteristic as expressed by words. The "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the distinction intended by the speaker's intention. For example, "because it is real" is the specific characteristic of the *dharmin*;
"matter (*rūpa*) definitely separated from visual consciousness" versus "matter not definitely separated from visual consciousness" is the distinction of the *dharmin*. Definite...

The thesis is that [the object] is not separate from visual consciousness; this is the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon. That the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is necessarily not separate from the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is a specific property (*viśeṣa*) of that phenomenon.

As for "contradiction" (*viruddha*), it refers to a reason that contradicts the thesis. Generally, when a contradictory reason is presented as a fallacy, it is formulated as a formal inference (*pramāṇa*).
All change their school but not their cause. What was different becomes identical; what was identical becomes different. It appears that the former commentators did not understand this.
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics.
Among these, the reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property to be proven (*dharma*) is as follows:

for example, one might say, "Sound is permanent, because it is produced, or because it is an effect of volitional effort. This reason exists only in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); therefore, it is contradictory.
This reason contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the subsequent thesis. For example, to say:
"Sound is eternal, because it is produced" (which is the fourth of the nine types of *pakṣadharmas*), or "because it is produced by volitional effort" (the sixth of the nine).
This reason exists only in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), because [sound] is eternal.
Regarding the established tenet: one must necessarily take space and the like as the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and jars, bowls, and the like as the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Now, the reason "being produced" (or "arising from volitional effort") functions only with respect to the dissimilar class such as jars, and does not function with respect to the similar class such as space;
therefore, it contradicts the essential characteristic of the permanent tenet itself.

Regarding the reason that contradicts the specific qualification of the thesis (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddhahetu*): for example, [the claim] that the eyes and so forth (the self-characteristic of the thesis) necessarily exist for the sake of another (the specific qualification of the thesis).

Because it is accumulative in nature (this is the contradictory reason). For example, bedding and so forth (this is the illustration; the formal proof is established above, and the contradiction is demonstrated below). This reason is capable of establishing [the point].

The eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another (this "other" is none other than the self). In this way, one can also establish a contradiction with the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) of the thesis to be proven (first stating the fault, then explaining the reason).
Various items such as bedding and furniture exist for the sake of another aggregate (this "other" belongs to another person), because they are used for the enjoyment of another aggregate.
This reason contradicts the specific characteristic intended by the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the subsequent thesis.
The *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya) states: "The Self (*ātman*) is substantially existent, because it exists for the sake of another.
I observe that all aggregations in the world exist for the sake of another; for example, aggregations such as beds and seats do not exist for their own use."
They must all be established for the sake of a person; it is because another can utilize them that they are gathered together.

This applies likewise to houses and the like, and likewise to the "great" [elements] and so forth (the "great" refers to earth, water, fire, wind, and space; "and so forth" refers to the remaining twenty-two dharmas). The collection of the five great elements is called the body (*kāya*).
This body does not exist for its own sake; one must know with certainty that it exists for the sake of another. That "other" is precisely the self; therefore, one knows that the self truly exists.
Herein, we borrow their own terminology to establish a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute them.

Taking the single element of the eye within the "body"—which is the name given to the collection of the five great elements—as the subject (*dharmin*), the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it does not exist for its own use but is entirely for the sake of another. [The reason is] "because it is a collection."
The collection [of atoms] constitutes the reason (*hetu*). Beds, seats, and the like serve as the concordant examples (*sapakṣa*).
Now, it goes without saying that the eye is not of the same category as beds and seats; nor is it without saying that the accumulation of the eye differs from the accumulation of beds and seats.
For now, let us debate this solely on the basis of what is called "the other" (*para*). First, it is said that these are not for one's own use, but must all be established for the sake of others.
Then there is a distinction between self and other. Later, it is said that "the other" is precisely the self; thus, there is no distinction between self and other.
If one wishes to accomplish the accumulation of the body, one blends self and other into one.

If one wishes to accomplish the accumulation of bedding and requisites, one analyzes self and other into two. Is this not a contradiction? Self and other are precisely what constitutes differentiation. Therefore...
This is the reason for the nature of being an aggregate (*saṃghātatva*).

Just as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)—that the eye and so forth must necessarily exist for the sake of another—is established, it also establishes the fault of contradicting the specific qualification of that subject-property. Why?
Because aggregates such as beds and seats produced by craftsmen are exclusively for the enjoyment of the owner of the aggregate; therefore, the eye is an aggregate.
Maturation (*vipāka*) and nurturance (*aupacayika*) are both not subject to others; how could they possibly be of that same category?

Even the making of beds and the weaving of mats have instances where one uses them for oneself. To exclude this portion, it says: "accumulated for the use of others, such as bedding and so forth. To state the contradiction with the formal argument (*pramāṇa*), it says:
"The eyes and so forth are not for the use of others, because they possess the nature of being accumulated, just like the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). This is the *dharmin*.
The "floating dust-sense" (the physical organ) is the metaphor; the "ultimate sense" (the subtle faculty) is the referent.

An example of a reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) is as follows: [Thesis] That which has existence (*sat*) is neither substance (*dravya*), nor quality (*guṇa*), nor activity (*karman*). [Reason] Because it exists.
Because there is a real entity (the reason), because there are qualities and actions (the reason), just as in the case of "sameness-and-difference" (the example).

Just as this reason can establish the negation of [the categories of] substance and so forth (the thesis of non-substance, non-quality, and non-action), so too can it establish the negation of existence (the universal property of Great Existence).
This is because both [negations] are equally certain (since it can negate this certainty, it likewise negates that).
This reason contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) stated in the thesis. The Vaiśeṣika masters establish six categories (*padārtha*):

1) substance (*dravya*), 2) quality (*guṇa*), 3) action (*karman*), 4) the nature of existence (*sattā*), 5) the nature of sameness-and-difference (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), and 6) the nature of inherence (*samavāya*).

Each possesses its own intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*), and they differ in the number of phenomena they subsume. Among these, the nature of existence (*sattā*) is unique, while substance, quality, and action—these three—[subsume many phenomena].
Because they share the same existence (*sattā*), there exists a distinct dharma as an entity apart from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).

Due to this Great Existence (*mahāsattā*), substances and the others are said to "exist. Likewise, the commonality (*sāmānya*) is also one; it is the single commonality shared by the three—substance, quality, and action.

However, apart from substance and the others, there exists a separate real entity (as detailed in the eighth fascicle of the *Huayan xuantan* and the *Shengzong shiju lun*). What is here called the nature of existence (*sattva*) is precisely that.

The fourth is the nature of *mahāsattā* (Great Existence). To speak of the "nature of existence" (*sattā-svabhāva*) means that the term "existence-nature" directly denotes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the nature of Great Existence (as it does not yet discuss the distinctions of whether this nature is existent or non-existent, etc.). It is neither substance (*dravya*), nor quality (*guṇa*), nor activity (*karman*).
Its thesis (*pakṣa*) is that there exists a distinct, real entity (*vastu*) apart from those substances, qualities, and activities; it takes these three—substance, quality, and activity—as its basis.

There exists that which has a real entity (*dravya*) as its cause. Because it possesses the nature of a real quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), or substance (*dravya*) in itself, it is not those [qualities, actions, or substances] themselves.
Using "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) as an analogy: sameness-and-difference possesses a real entity of sameness-and-difference, yet it is not a real entity and so forth.

This clarifies that existence (*astitva*) possesses a real entity of existence, yet it is not a real entity and so forth. However, since this [existence] has "possessing a real entity" and so forth as its cause...
In establishing the refutation of categories such as "substance" (*dravya*), one also establishes the refutation of "existence" (*sattā*).

This, however, contradicts the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), because [the opponent] asserts that substance, quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) are identical with existence. Since you refute the nature of substance and so forth, do you not thereby refute the nature of great existence (*mahāsattā*)?
For both the refutation of this and the refutation of that are equally certain. To state the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) for the contradiction: Existence is...
Substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karma*) are identical; for there is one substance, and there are qualities and activities. As it is said regarding the son of a barren woman:

"The *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* states that [the categories] share the common meaning of being conjoined with substance, quality, and activity; they serve as the causes for the cognition of their designations."

If difference (*anyatva*) were identical to permanence (*nitya*) and substantiality (*dravya*), etc., then the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) would have a single reality as its nature, which would negate the meaning of cognition.

In this treatise, the analogy of "sameness and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) is cited; there is a profound intention therein. It is like [the case where] "sameness" intends to conjoin, while "difference" conversely negates it.

Herein, the two characters *cheng* (establish) and *ze* (negate) are precisely those characters for *he* (conjoin) and *ze* (negate). This metaphor illustrates that there exists a separate reality of substance, quality, and activity.
The original intention was to establish a thesis by synthesizing these factors into a functional entity, yet one instead negates its very essence through contradiction.

Thus, we know that this "nature of identity and difference," as well as the analogies of the bedding and so forth, may be treated as definitely present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) before the contradictory meaning is presented;
however, once the contradictory meaning is set forth, they are reversed and become entirely absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, they are not altered.
The two members—the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—serve merely to exclude the contradictory nature of the reason (*hetu*).
Regarding the "reason that contradicts a qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddhahetu*):

This is the thesis within the context of the "pervasive absence of nature" in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Because it is a provisional designation based on a locus that lacks material obstruction, although there are empty words, there is no real object at all.

Because it is for the purpose of establishing the meaning [of the thesis], even though one does not posit the existence of a substantial great void (*mahā-ākāśa*) and so forth in opposition [to the thesis], one is still able to demonstrate that there is no locus for the thesis and that the meaning of "absence of cause" is established.

This [position] is not accepted in part. How is it proven that space being permanent is not accepted as a common example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the thesis (*pakṣa*)? It is said:
The *Śataśāstra*, in the "Chapter on Refuting Permanence," states: "Although they employ diligent expedients to establish permanence, they ultimately fail to provide a reasoned argument.

This point is sometimes obscured and sometimes revealed throughout this treatise. Indeed, once the three-membered inference was established, the extreme views and the view of a self held by the heterodox outsiders [were overturned].

The *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ten Categories) states: What is the category of action (*karma-pada*)? It refers to five kinds of action, which constitute the category of action.

that which depends on a single real entity is called the activity of relinquishing. What is the activity of bending (*ākuñcana-karma*)? It refers to [the action] regarding the great...

What is the action of extension (*prasāraṇa-karma*)? It refers to when a large, long, substantial entity relies upon a single substance, there is conjunction at the proximal points, and [simultaneously] there is the cause for the separation of near and distant points;

However, if one says, "All things that possess resistance are impermanent," then the fault remains hidden. This is because...
Because all material entities are impermanent, this inversion is a fault because it deviates from that [truth].
