therefore, it is said that there are only two authorities. △ Second, the actual explanation.
Among these, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).

If there is correct cognition regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*), it is called direct perception because it operates by manifesting each [object] distinctly, being devoid of all conceptual constructions such as names and categories.
An ancient master’s commentary explains: Regarding "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*), "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifesting;

it refers to clearly realizing an object without the mediation of names and conventions, without a mind of conjecture, and by personally attaining the essence of the phenomenon while remaining free from false conceptualization—this is termed "direct.

As for "perception" (*pramāṇa*), it means measuring; it carries the sense of definitive determination. It refers to the mind measuring and definitively determining a phenomenon with respect to its object.
Because its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is non-erroneous, it is called "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). The essence of true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists of:

the mental consciousness associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), all self-verifying portions (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), all meditative minds, and the eighth consciousness. These various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are termed "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of six meanings:

first, they are "presently existing," which excludes things such as a tortoise's hair; second, they are "present in time," which excludes the past and future; third, they are "manifestly appearing," which excludes... [text truncated]
1. Seed (*bīja*): Because it lacks functional activity. 2. Manifest (*pratyakṣa*): "Manifest" refers to manifest illumination.

This means the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of the cognizing mind, which is far removed from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). That is to say, this refers to non-conceptualization and so forth. 3. Manifest (*pratyakṣa*): This refers to luminous manifestation.
It means that when the various meditative minds are clear and tranquil, whatever object they encounter, they realize it with clarity. That is to say, luminosity.

The direct realization of various objects is termed *pratyakṣa* (direct perception). "Sixfold direct perception" refers to immediate manifestation; that is, the immediate and intimate realization of its own essence.

Whether it be all states of distracted mind or the immediate engagement with an object, whenever there is a clear and intimate realization of its own essence, it is all termed *pratyakṣa*. This is the fifth [section], the clarification of direct perception.

The sixth is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). These two types [of direct perception] distinguish themselves from various forms of erroneous cognition, such as the vision of floating hairs or flowers in the sky by those with diseased eyes.
Although these latter cognitions are free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), they cannot clearly realize objects or directly encounter their own essence;

therefore, they are not direct perception. Regarding the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), ancient commentaries provide roughly two interpretations: first, "the measure of what is manifest" (*pratyakṣasya pramāṇam*).
This refers to the first five consciousnesses. Depending upon their respective bases (the sense organs), they take presently existing objects as their cognitive range in the present time.

The sense organs also, together with the consciousnesses, illuminate the external objects; they possess the functional capacity to produce consciousness, and because the meaning of "organ" (*indriya*) is preeminent, they receive the name "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*).

Although they illuminate objects, because their essence is matter (*rūpa*), they lack the function of conceptualization (*saṃtīraṇa*); they cannot perform measurement or judgment, but possess only the sense of "manifestation. They do not [possess the nature of]... [inference].

That which is called "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers exclusively to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). They are termed "direct" because they measure their objects; their function of cognitive engagement (*ālambana*) is predominant, and their essence possesses the sense of being manifest.

Furthermore, they possess the capacity to perceive objects directly. Now, following the perspective of the originating faculty, the resulting consciousness is designated as "direct perception," employing the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Second, "the manifest is itself the means of valid cognition" (*pratyakṣam eva pramāṇam*), referring to a portion of the clearly discerning mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), excluding other distracted states.

Regarding the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and that which arises independently (*mukhyotthita*), these include the mental consciousness in meditative absorption as well as the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

These take the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of their respective objects of cognition as their direct object. While their functioning manifests [as the perceiving subject], the substantial essence (*dravya*) of their supporting faculty—the mind-base (*manas-indriya*)—does not manifest;

therefore, it is not included. Rather, with respect to the seeing-portion that acts as the cognizer, the manifestation itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Furthermore, "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*) indicates the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the cognitive subject (*ālambaka*):

it does not deliberate or evaluate, but functions spontaneously and effortlessly, reflecting in accordance with its preceding object. "Free from all conceptualization regarding names, categories, and so forth" means being free from the conceptualizing mind that involves recollection, deliberation, and various gateways such as names and categories.
(Briefly, there are three types of conceptualization: first, conceptualization by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), which [functions] solely by...)

Present conceptualization (*nirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) is the conceptualization that operates upon the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) currently being perceived as objects. These perceived objects are the five sensory domains (*pañca-viṣaya*). Regarding the operation upon specific characteristics: for example, when visual consciousness perceives color, it takes "blue" as its mode of operation; because it functions spontaneously toward the mode of blue, it is called "self-operation.

Furthermore, the specific characteristic is itself the operation of the perceiving subject, which distinguishes it from the operation upon general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). For instance, when perceiving blue, one does not simultaneously apprehend yellow. Second is recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), which is the conceptualization that follows and recollects the various conditioned phenomena previously experienced. It perceives only the past.

Third is deliberative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), which is the conceptualization that constructs thoughts regarding the past, future, and present when they are not directly manifest. This consists of conceiving existence where there is no existence; it is an object that is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nevertheless, it deliberates across the three times and is not restricted to a single time. Self-... [text ends]

"Discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is itself non-discrimination. Regarding "manifesting and turning separately": in the present life, by means of a manifesting mind, one takes a presently existing object as its condition;
it turns only in accordance with the discrimination of the intrinsic nature of that which is conditioned. If this is so, why is it called "non-discriminative"? It is said:

although the discrimination of intrinsic nature exists, because the other two [types of discrimination] are absent, it is called "non-discriminative. This is like a horse with only one leg being called [a "one-legged horse"].

Regarding "being without satisfaction," the drowsy words say: "This direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the subsequent inference (*anumāna*), according to the verse, should appear later in the text following the refutation of the pseudo-inference (*ābhāsa*).
That it is established within the treatise is because the Master of the Treatise wishes for people to realize the methods of establishing and refuting;
this is precisely to accomplish the matters within this direct perception. If a person thoroughly understands this essence, based on..."
Based on the former, one may establish a proof; based on the latter, one may effect a refutation. Were it otherwise, it would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Based on the former, it constitutes a fallacious proof (*pratipakṣa-ābhāsa*); based on the latter, it becomes a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇa-ābhāsa*). Therefore, it is placed here.

This is shown to those who establish tenets and compose treatises: they must flow forth from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) before they are fit to act as masters of proof and refutation.
△ Fourth, the section on the gate of true inference (*anumāna*), in two parts. First, the formal explanation.
Regarding inference (*anumāna*): it refers to observing an object by means of its various characteristics (*liṅga*). There are three types of characteristics, as previously explained.
With these as causes, there arises correct knowledge regarding the object to be inferred, such as the cognition that "there is fire" or "it is impermanent," and so forth.
This is called inference (*anumāna*). Regarding "inference":
*anu* means analogy (*anvaya*), and *māna* means measurement (*pariccheda*). It is called inference because it is known to exist through analogical measurement.
"The various characteristics" refers to the three types of characteristics. The three types of characteristics are: that which is entirely the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
These are the three characteristics [of a valid reason]: being necessarily present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and entirely absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Based on these three characteristics as the cause, correct knowledge arises regarding the meaning of the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-anumāna*). Regarding the phrase "understanding, etc.," one should know that there are five types of inference: first, characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); second, essence (*svabhāva*);
third, function (*karma*); fourth, property (*dharma*); and fifth, cause and effect (*hetu-phala*). As for the first, inference by characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-anumāna*), it is as follows:
It follows the characteristics and their mutual relations as they exist, or it proceeds from the present and from previously inferred objects—
such as inferring the existence of a chariot because one sees its banner, or inferring the existence of fire because one sees smoke.
As for inference based on the nature of two entities (*svabhāvānumāna*), it consists in inferring an unperceived object by virtue of having directly perceived its essential nature.
Substance (*dravya*). Or, one may perceive a portion of its own substance and infer the remaining portions by analogy, such as inferring the past and future based on the present.
Regarding inference through action (*karma-anumāna*), this refers to inferring the substratum of an action based on the action itself;

for example, seeing an object at a distance that does not move, yet has birds perched upon it, one infers it is a tree stump (*sthāṇu*); whereas if there were movement, one would infer it is otherwise.
Regarding these persons, the fourfold inference (*anumāna*) refers to inferring the remainder from one [attribute] among all mutually connected phenomena.
For example: by virtue of being connected with impermanence, one infers that there is suffering; by virtue of being connected with suffering, one infers emptiness and non-self;

by virtue of being connected with birth, one infers the presence of the phenomenon of aging; and by virtue of being connected with aging, one infers the presence of the phenomenon of death, and so forth. Fifth is the inference of cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-anumāna*).
Inference (*anumāna*) refers to the comparison of cause and effect. For example, seeing a person walking, one infers that they have reached a destination;

seeing that they have reached a destination, one infers that they previously walked. If one sees a person serving a king according to the Dharma, one infers that they shall obtain vast rank and emolument;
seeing great rank and emolument, one infers that they previously served a king according to the Dharma and so forth. To clearly know that fire exists [is likewise].

Regarding "inference" (*anumāna*): to thoroughly know impermanence through inference is "inference of phenomena" (*dharmanumāna*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes other [categories] such as essence, activity, cause, and effect.
The *Yuyan* (Sleeping Words) states: "The first gate above, 'Direct Perception' (*pratyakṣa*), corresponds to the two characters 'Correct Principle' (*nyāya*) in the title;
this present gate, 'Inference' (*anumāna*), corresponds to the two characters 'Hetuvidyā' in the title. Therefore, the method of inference is entirely [based upon] direct perception."

The function of wisdom within the essence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from that essence; thus, it is designated as the "cause" (*hetu*). When this function is subsumed back into the essence, it is called "entering the principle" (*tattva-praveśa*).

It should be understood that this true inference (*tarka-pramāṇa*) is precisely what is derived from the "reason" (*hetu*) among the three members of the formal proof (*sādhana*), specifically from the method of the three characteristics (*trirūpa*). △ Second, the general conclusion.

Within the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cognition itself is called the "result" (*phala*) because it is the characteristic of realization; it is also called a "valid cognition" because it manifests as having an operative function.

Within these two types of valid cognition, this is the general statement: that cognition itself is called the result because it is the characteristic of realization—this is what is meant by "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
Because it manifests with a functional activity, it is also termed a "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*); specifically, it is called "inference" (*anumāna*).
Wisdom itself is the result; it receives its name by way of identity with its function (*dharmadharmivācya*), for it is the mode of apprehension that realizes the truth.

From the time an ordinary person perceives a real object with a sudden, impulsive mind, all such instances constitute direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When, through hearing the ultimate teaching, correct wisdom arises, one attains...

The self-characteristic of phenomena is also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), continuing even up to the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the wisdom that takes this as its object, there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended;
wisdom and suchness are equal and identical, which is likewise nothing but direct perception. Direct perception does not admit of duality.
How could wisdom not be identical with its fruit? It is like the sense organs, such as the eye; they are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) only by Buddhas and the like.

In the distracted minds of others, they are not apprehended through direct perception, because [the organ] possesses activity insofar as it can give rise to consciousness; thus, its existence is known through inference (*anumāna*).
Although this is inferential knowledge, it does not contradict the direct perception of a Buddha. However, since the organ is material form (*rūpa*), it lacks the capacity for cognition.

Regarding "consideration" (*ālambana*): because it manifests, it also carries the sense of "manifesting. Since that which lacks consideration cannot be termed a "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), only this inferential knowledge (*anumāna*) is designated as valid cognition.
Both "function" (*kāritra*) and "manifestation" refer to the sense faculty (*indriya*).

By analogy with the sense faculty, although the faculty itself lacks the status of valid cognition, it is supplemented by saying it is "also called valid cognition. This is the explanation of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla.
There are phenomena in the world that can be summarized into three types: first, phenomena known through direct perception, such as form, sound, and so forth;
second, phenomena experienced through use, such as jars, clothing, and so forth; third, phenomena possessing functional activity, such as the eyes, ears, and so forth.

While objects such as form and sound are commonly perceived by the world and obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the five sense faculties, such as the eyes, are not obtained through direct perception because of them.

That [object] is known to exist through inference (*anumāna*). This uses a phenomenon possessing functional activity as an illustration of true inference (*bhūtānumāna*), while treating the objects of current experience as pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

Since one sees that true inference does not contradict perception, then all that the world calls "inference" is merely non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Is it not evident, then, how this reveals the correct and shuts out the erroneous?
How profound and penetrating this explanation is! △ Fifth, the gate of what resembles direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Discursive cognition that operates in a manner different from the object is called "resembling direct perception. This refers to all cognitions that arise through the conceptualization of jars, clothing, and so forth;
because they do not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objective domain with respect to the object, they are called resembling direct perception.

This means that all cognitions of the wise arise from the conceptualization of jars, clothes, and so forth. This explains the aforementioned "discriminative cognition," because such cognition does not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
This explains the aforementioned "functioning differently with respect to the object. Regarding the phrase "cognizing jars, clothes, and so forth":
although these are currently perceived and utilized, they are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are conventional (*prajñapti*) phenomena.

The mind that takes a jar or the like as its object does not take its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, because it takes its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is known only by realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*) and is beyond the reach of verbal expression, this is the specific characteristic. If the essence of a phenomenon is within the reach of verbal expression and is the object of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), this is the general characteristic.
For example, when visual consciousness takes the specific characteristic of a blue object as its object, it apprehends the color blue.
Regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): when a subsequent moment of conceptualizing mental consciousness arises, it is no longer a cognition of the blue color itself;

rather, it is a conceptual construction based on common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). At the very moment such a cognitive act occurs, the actual substance of the blue color is not present, as it is accompanied by names and expressions (*nāma-pada*).
This is a cognition of a false appearance (*bhrānti*). Question: To which type of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this mind that takes a jar or a garment as its object subsumed? Answer:

Because it does not directly apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the dharma, it is not true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Because it is not an inferential estimation, it is also not inference (*anumāna*). It is therefore subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Alternatively, those who claim that a semblance of direct perception (*pratibhāsa-pratyakṣābhāsa*) is identical to true inference are incorrect. Zhi Jue says: "A semblance of direct perception..."
Regarding "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*): according to reason, there are five kinds of cognition that are all termed "pseudo-perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

First, a distracted mind taking the past as its object; second, the solitary mental consciousness taking the present as its object; third, a distracted mental consciousness taking the future as its object; fourth, a cognition of doubt regarding the three periods of time;
and fifth, various deluded understandings taking the present as their object. These various states of mind possess cognitive modes (*ākāra*) that involve deliberation.

Because they transcend [the object], none of them take their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objective domain. Furthermore, because they arise through the transformation of conceptualization based on what was previously experienced, they are termed "resembling direct perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
There are two types: first, non-conceptual [cognition], which refers to the class of ignorant people, as well as the spontaneous perception of things such as flowers in the sky.
Although these lack conceptualization, they do not clearly ascertain the object, but rather apprehend it obscurely.

It is called "pseudo-direct perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). Second, there is the conceptual mind which, while currently bearing names and phrases, fails to grasp the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon;
yet it falsely claims to clearly apprehend the essence of the object. This is called pseudo-direct perception.

Furthermore, it is said that seeing a unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*), such as "man," "woman," "heaven," or "earth," is called pseudo-direct perception. This is because [such an object] is a combination of many conditions, just like gathering together many atoms (*paramāṇu*).
It is formed from form. When the five aggregates combine to constitute a person, it is called a "composite mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*).
One who views things in this way possesses a conceptualizing cognition that functions erroneously with respect to its object; therefore, it is termed "pseudo-perception.

As for true perception, such a composite mark cannot be apprehended as a mark. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata speaks of a 'composite mark,' yet it is not a composite."

The Conjunction of Characteristics: Because it arises from the conjunction of conditions, it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This nature of being devoid of intrinsic nature is the principle to be realized.
To know it thus is the arising of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*); it functions within its own characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) and is called true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
6. The Gate of Fallacious Inference (*tarka-ābhāsa*).
If there is a cognition based on a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), the resulting cognitions of objects that appear to be real are called "fallacious inference" (*tarka*).

There are many types of fallacious reasons as previously explained; when these are employed as causes, various cognitions arise regarding fallacious objects of inference (*anumeya*) that are unable to provide correct understanding.
It is called "pseudo-inference" (*anumānābhāsa*).
Because there are many types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), the cognition of pseudo-reasons is explained as having fourteen faults; thus it is said to be "of many kinds.

Taking those as the reasons, the preceding [explanation] is established first. Nāgārjuna also said: "Because it evolves through conceptualization according to what was previously perceived. This must be so.
It refers to the seeds of false views contained within the eight consciousnesses. When these manifest as active functioning (*samudācāra*), they constitute "pseudo-knowledge" (*tulyārtha-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "pseudo-object of inference" (*tulyārtha-anumeya*) below, this explains the meaning of "pseudo" in the aforementioned "pseudo-knowledge. That is to say, when various cognitions arise in accordance with that pseudo-reason (*hetu*) and the pseudo-object of inference, it is termed "pseudo-object-knowledge.
Alternatively, it may refer collectively to the pseudo-establishment [of the thesis], naming it the "pseudo-reason," in relation to [the object].
Because it is the fruit of cognition: whenever cognition arises, it is itself the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). **7.
The Section on True Refutation.** Furthermore, if one correctly demonstrates the faults in the proof (*sādhana*), it is called "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).

This refers to: first, the nature of deficiency in the proof (the thirty-three faults collectively termed "deficiency"); the nature of faults in the thesis (*pakṣa*) (the nine faults within the thesis); the nature of an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*); and the nature of an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*).

It is called "destructive" (*dūṣaṇa*) because it demonstrates the nature of contradictory reasons (the fourteen fallacies among reasons) and the nature of fallacious examples (the ten fallacies among examples),
thereby instructing and enlightening the questioner.
As for what is called "refutation," why should one strive for such a task? It is intended solely to awaken the questioner and cause them to give rise to right knowledge.
The mind of the refuter is a mind of compassion; it is a vast mind.

Otherwise, if one merely displays the faults of the opponent, destroys the other's tenet, and establishes one's own tenet, that does not constitute true refutation—how much less so to leave things as they are!

Huìyún: If one does not state that [the argument] causes the other to understand, then as long as the listener has not yet understood this meaning, it should be termed the "establishment of a thesis" (*pakṣa*).

In that case, the questioner would not comprehend it, and the thesis itself would not be established; how, then, could it constitute a valid refutation? △ Eight: The Section on Fallacious Refutations.
If one expresses words that falsely indicate a flaw in the proof (*sādhana*), it is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
This refers to stating that a complete proof is deficient (this is the general definition). It includes stating that a faultless thesis (*pakṣa*) has a fault;
stating that an established reason (*hetu*) is unestablished; stating that a determinate reason is indeterminate; and stating that a non-contradictory reason is contradictory. Regarding...
To state a flawless analogy as a flawed one—such verbal expression is called a "pseudo-refutation," for it cannot reveal the faults of another's position, since that [position] is without fault.
Let us now leave this matter aside.
There is originally no deficiency; yet, by falsely claiming there is a deficiency, one fails to establish the opponent's thesis and instead turns it into a fault of one's own.
Therefore, this is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*). The final phrase concludes the discussion and summarizes the argument.
In Nāgārjuna’s treatise, the characteristics of pseudo-refutations are presented extensively; as the text is voluminous, it is not cited here. △ Third, the verse conclusion.

Having briefly proclaimed the meaning of a few phrases to establish the initial orientation of the quarters, the principles of what is logical and what is illogical will be subtly debated in other sections, beginning with verses and concluding with verses;
this is the essence of a treatise (*śāstra*). At the end of Nāgārjuna’s treatise, it is also said: "Furthermore, this very..."
Regarding fallacious arguments (*jāti-dūṣaṇa*), I have already extensively refuted them within my own works on the *Nyāya-śāstra* and other treatises.
Furthermore, I have already analyzed this topic in detail within the ancient Indian treatises on logic (*hetuvidyā*). Therefore, let us now desist.
It should be known that there are many excellent treatises on the single school of Hetuvidyā; those of which the Sanskrit originals have flowed into China number in the hundreds and thousands.
There are only one or two [extant]. Of the thirty-six sections that Master Xuanzang brought back, there are now only these two or three remaining in the canon, and they are sparse indeed.
Furthermore, readers do not engage in precise or extensive study;

wishing to fathom the realm of the Buddha’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with their shallow and discursive minds, how can they avoid the fault of slandering the Dharma? This principle is the very truth.
To claim that "establishing the true" (立真) and "refuting the false" (破非理) constitute what are merely "pseudo-establishment" (似立) and "pseudo-refutation" (似破) is incorrect.

According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, in addition to the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and application (*upanaya*), there is further what is called the conclusion (*nigamana*).
This refers to the correct statement made upon reaching the ultimate point, by which means the matter is thoroughly established through this reasoning; therefore, this [conclusion] is definitive.
There is certainly no difference; this is the final synthesis, which is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

For example, regarding those who maintain the doctrine of non-self (*anātman-vādin*), in reference to this very matter, one first states to the proponents of self (*ātman-vādin*) that all phenomena are without self; this statement constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Next, one states that if [the self] were designated in relation to the aggregates (*skandha*), four faults would be incurred; this statement constitutes the reason (*hetu*). Why is this so? If, in regard to...

Regarding those who designate a real self within the aggregates (*skandha*): is this conceived self identical with the characteristics of the aggregates, or does it exist within the aggregates, or elsewhere, or is it designated as something unrelated to the aggregates?

If it is designated as being identical with the characteristics of the aggregates, then since the aggregates lack self-mastery, arise from a multitude of conditions, and are subject to arising and ceasing, the self would likewise be so. If it were identical with those characteristics, the self would not [be permanent].

This would be the first fault. If [the self] were designated within the aggregates, then since the aggregates which serve as its basis are impermanent, the self that depends upon them would also have to be impermanent; this is the second fault.
If it were designated in a location separate from the aggregates, the self would have no cause and would be purposeless; this is the third fault. If not...

If the self were designated in dependence upon the aggregates, it would exist independently; being liberated by its own nature, it would seek liberation again, thereby rendering its effort futile—this is the fourth fault.
Next, it is said that as one designates the past based on the present, this statement serves as an illustration. Why is this?
If the past were designated as truly existent in the same manner as the characteristics of the present, [it would follow that it is likewise subject to change].
Regarding this conceived "past": is it identical to the characteristic of the present? Does it exist within the present? Does it exist elsewhere?

Or is it designated without depending upon the present? If it is designated as being identical to the characteristic of the present, then since that which has already arisen but not yet ceased constitutes the characteristic of the present, the essence of past phenomena would likewise have to possess the characteristic of having already arisen but not yet ceased.
This is the first fault. If it were designated within the present, then to designate the essence of cessation within that which has not yet ceased would be inconsistent and therefore unreasonable;

this is the second fault. If it were designated elsewhere apart from the present, then apart from the present, not even a slight portion of any other truly existent conditioned phenomenon can be found. How [could it exist]?

To designate [it] as such in relation to that [past] is the third fault. If one were to designate it without depending on the present, then one would also have to designate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the past;
this is the fourth fault. However, because the characteristics of the past have ceased and perished, the meaning of "absence of characteristics" is established.
If one were to designate it as being the same as the present, then these four faults would ensue. Therefore, [the past is not designated].
The characteristic of passing away is not established. It is the same for the selflessness of all phenomena.
If one were to designate a self in relation to the aggregates, four faults would ensue; therefore, the meaning of selflessness is established.

Having thus explained the refutation of the inversion of a self, it follows by this very principle that permanence and so forth also do not exist. This statement is a transition to what follows. By this principle, therefore:

"The five aggregates are all impermanent," up to "they are selfless"—this statement constitutes a conclusion (*nigamana*). If one knows that there is no conclusion because [the parts] are merely joined together, then it would not be ultimate;
how, then, could it constitute a proof (*sādhana*) or a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*)? Therefore, it is set forth explicitly.
The Treatise on Entering into Right Theory through Logic (Concluded)
